nodes.title: The conductor of a Weil–Deligne representation, with its monodromy term
nodes.statement: Let K be a nonarchimedean local field (tier (F) of R01.3/breaks-and-swan-conductor) with residue cardinality q, W_K its Weil group (ClassFieldTheory layer 9) and (r, N) a Weil–Deligne representation of W_K on a finite-dimensional vector space V over a field F of characteristic 0 (R01.2/weil-deligne-representation: r continuous with r(I_K) finite, N nilpotent, r(w) N r(w)^{-1} = q^{v'(w)} N with v'(arithmetic Frobenius lift) = 1). ker N is r(W_K)-stable and r(I_K) acts on it. Define a(r, N) := Sw(r) + dim V − dim (ker N)^{r(I_K)}, where Sw(r) is the Swan conductor of r|_{P_K} (R01.3/breaks-and-swan-conductor, which only uses G_K^u ⊆ P_K ⊆ W_K for u > 0). Equivalently a(r, N) = a(r) + dim V^{r(I_K)} − dim (ker N)^{r(I_K)}, with a(r) = codim V^{r(I_K)} + Sw(r) the conductor of r alone. Comparison: for ℓ ≠ p, F = E finite over Q_ℓ (or Q̄_ℓ) and ρ: G_K → GL(V) continuous with WD(ρ) = (r, N) (R01.2/grothendieck-monodromy-and-the-weil-deligne-functor), a(ρ) = a(r, N), independently of the Frobenius lift and of the homomorphism t_ℓ used to build WD(ρ); and a(r, N) = a(r^{F-ss}, N) for the Frobenius semisimplification (R01.2/frobenius-semisimplification).
hypotheses: finite residue field (the Weil group needs the Frobenius); characteristic-0 coefficients
the monodromy term is dim V^{r(I_K)} − dim (ker N)^{r(I_K)} ≥ 0; it is not dim V − dim ker N
proofSteps: (ker N) is stable: r(w)N r(w)^{-1} is a nonzero multiple of N. For σ ∈ I_K, v'(σ) = 0, so r(σ) commutes with N.

a(ρ) = a(WD(ρ)): Sw(ρ) = Sw(r) because ρ and r agree on P_K (t_ℓ is trivial on P_K); and V^{ρ(I_K)} = (ker N)^{r(I_K)} (R01.3/artin-conductor-with-its-wild-part), so codim V^{ρ(I_K)} = dim V − dim (ker N)^{r(I_K)} (Ulmer 2016 §8: the definitions of Deligne and Serre agree).
Independence of choices and Frobenius semisimplification: both only change r on W_K \ I_K or by conjugation, and the formula only involves r|_{I_K} and ker N.
acceptance: sp(2): r unramified and N ≠ 0 (rank one): a = 0 + 2 − 1 = 1 (Steinberg exponent 1); sp(n) ⊗ (unramified χ), n ≥ 1: a = n − 1
sp(2) ⊗ χ with χ ramified: (ker N)^{r(I_K)} = 0, so a = 2·a(χ) (e.g. = 2 for χ tamely ramified)
The ℓ-adic Tate module of a Tate curve has WD = sp(2)-type with a = 1, agreeing with R01.3/artin-conductor-with-its-wild-part

uses.how: a(r, N) = a(r) + dim V^{I} − dim (ker N)^{I}; a = 1 for the Steinberg parameter, giving KW I §8.4's dyadic bound

nodes.title: Global conductors and the prime-to-p conductor N(ρ̄)
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field and ρ: G_F → GL(V) a continuous representation (R01.1) on a finite-dimensional vector space over a field C_ρ, unramified outside a finite set of places (R01.2/unramified-and-ramification-set). Let Σ be a finite set of finite places of F containing every finite place whose residue characteristic is the characteristic of C_ρ if that characteristic is positive, and every place above ℓ if ρ is ℓ-adic (C_ρ ⊆ Q̄_ℓ with the ℓ-adic topology); Σ may be empty for an Artin representation (C_ρ = C, finite image). For v ∉ Σ let a_v(ρ) := a(ρ|_{G_{F_v}}) (R01.2/local-restriction, R01.3/artin-conductor-with-its-wild-part; ρ(P_{F_v}) is finite at such v). The Σ-conductor is the ideal N^Σ(ρ) := ∏_{v ∉ Σ finite} 𝔭_v^{a_v(ρ)} of O_F (a finite product); N(ρ) := N^∅(ρ) for Artin representations; for ℓ-adic ρ, N^{(ℓ)}(ρ) := N^{{v | ℓ}}(ρ) is the prime-to-ℓ conductor (the exponent at v | ℓ is not defined in this layer). For ρ̄ over a finite field of characteristic p, N(ρ̄) := N^{{v | p}}(ρ̄) is the prime-to-p conductor; it is prime to p by construction. For F = Q every such ideal is identified with its positive generator, e.g. N(ρ̄) = ∏_{l ≠ p} l^{n(l, ρ̄)} (Serre 1987 (1.2.3)). Conductor notation applies to the specified representation itself; taking global semisimplification can lower its tame contribution. In the elliptic reduction formula use E[ℓ] before semisimplification.
hypotheses: the local exponent at v uses ρ restricted to a decomposition group through a chosen embedding ι_v; conjugate embeddings give isomorphic local representations and equal exponents
places in Σ are omitted, not given exponent 0 by convention: N(ρ̄) says nothing about ramification at p

The local conductor is used only in its established coefficient tiers: finite-image Artin representations, discrete coefficient fields of characteristic different from the residue characteristic, or ℓ-adic coefficients with the canonical ℓ-adic topology and ℓ different from that residue characteristic. In the last tier pass to a finite coefficient extension by R01.1 descent; arbitrary topological fields do not imply finite wild image.
proofSteps: a_v(ρ) = 0 for v unramified (R01.3/hasse-arf-integrality (c)), so the product is finite; integrality of each a_v from R01.3/hasse-arf-integrality.
Independence of ι_v: a different embedding conjugates the decomposition group, and the local conductor is an isomorphism invariant.
Over Q identify ideals of Z with positive integers through Ideal.absNorm / the generator.
acceptance: For the nontrivial character of Gal(Q(√−1)/Q), N = 4; for Ind_{G_{Q(√−1)}}^{G_Q} 1 = 1 ⊕ χ_{−4}, N = 4 = |d_{Q(√−1)}|
For E = 11a1 and ℓ = 5: N_E = 11 but N(ρ̄_{E,5}) = 1, because 5 divides v_11(Δ_min) = 5 (R01.3/residual-elliptic-conductor-away-from-ell)
For p odd, the mod-p cyclotomic character has N = 1 although it is ramified at p

the prime-to-ℓ residual conductor equals the deletion level and is prime to ℓ
the exact Artin conductor N(ρ) is the level of the weight-one newform

nodes.title: Swan additivity in exact sequences
nodes.statement: Let K be complete for a normalised discrete valuation with perfect residue field of characteristic p>0. Let F be a topological field of characteristic different from p, and V a finite-dimensional continuous F-representation of G_K with finite wild image. The arbitrary-perfect-residue-field case retains the recorded ramification-theory gap. For an exact sequence 0→V′→V→V″→0, Sw(V)=Sw(V′)+Sw(V″). In particular Sw(V)=Sw(Vˢˢ).
hypotheses: Let K be complete for a normalised discrete valuation with perfect residue field of characteristic p>0. Let F be a topological field of characteristic different from p, and V a finite-dimensional continuous F-representation of G_K with finite wild image. The arbitrary-perfect-residue-field case retains the recorded ramification-theory gap.
proofSteps: For every positive upper index the action factors through a finite p-group, whose order is invertible in F. Averaging makes invariants exact, hence codimensions additive; integrate the codimensions using R01.3/breaks-and-swan-conductor.
acceptance: This does not require semisimple tame inertia.

sources.locator: §2 (Preliminaries on conductors), after (2.1), printed p. 229 (PDF p. 4)
sources.match: Source context for Swan additivity in exact sequences. Brumer–Kramer call the conductor exponent (2.1) 'an additive function of V', for F of characteristic 0 or l ≠ p, and note that it is unchanged by extension of F (part (e)). Additivity holds on direct sums, and on exact sequences only when |G_0| is invertible in F (source issue E351); part (a) therefore states an inequality with its equality criterion. Their Lemma 2.4, on the same page, is the additivity of sw on exact sequences of part (a). The exact extracted statement and any generalisation are justified by this node’s proof plan, not by treating the source’s other bundle clauses as this declaration.

nodes.title: Artin conductor inequality for exact sequences
nodes.statement: Let K be complete for a normalised discrete valuation with perfect residue field of characteristic p>0. Let F be a topological field of characteristic different from p, and V a finite-dimensional continuous F-representation of G_K with finite wild image. The arbitrary-perfect-residue-field case retains the recorded ramification-theory gap. For an exact sequence 0→V′→V→V″→0, a(V)≥a(V′)+a(V″), with equality iff V^{I_K}→V″^{I_K} is onto. Artin conductors are additive on direct sums, and a(V)≥a(Vˢˢ).
hypotheses: Let K be complete for a normalised discrete valuation with perfect residue field of characteristic p>0. Let F be a topological field of characteristic different from p, and V a finite-dimensional continuous F-representation of G_K with finite wild image. The arbitrary-perfect-residue-field case retains the recorded ramification-theory gap.
proofSteps: Inertia invariants are left exact. Compute the defect of additivity of dim V−dim V^{I_K}; it is the cokernel dimension of V^{I_K}→V″^{I_K}. Combine with R01.3/swan-additive, and iterate along a composition series.
acceptance: A nontrivial unipotent tame extension of 1 by 1 has conductor one although its two constituents have conductor zero.

nodes.title: Conductors of dual representations
nodes.statement: Let K be complete for a normalised discrete valuation with perfect residue field of characteristic p>0. Let F be a topological field of characteristic different from p, and V a finite-dimensional continuous F-representation of G_K with finite wild image. The arbitrary-perfect-residue-field case retains the recorded ramification-theory gap. Sw(V∨)=Sw(V) and a(V∨)=a(V), even with infinite inertia image.
hypotheses: Let K be complete for a normalised discrete valuation with perfect residue field of characteristic p>0. Let F be a topological field of characteristic different from p, and V a finite-dimensional continuous F-representation of G_K with finite wild image. The arbitrary-perfect-residue-field case retains the recorded ramification-theory gap.
proofSteps: (b): V^∨ is the dual representation (Mathlib Representation.dual, R01.1/restriction-dual-tensor-twist). For a finite group H of order invertible in F, dim (V^∨)^H = dim V^H (the averaging idempotent is self-dual); this gives Sw(V^∨) = Sw(V) and (V^∨)^{P_K} = (V^{P_K})^∨. The quotient I_K/P_K is procyclic (LocalFieldsRamification layer 4); for a topological generator τ, continuity gives V^{I_K} = ker(ρ(τ) − 1 on V^{P_K}), and (V^∨)^{I_K} is the kernel of the transpose of ρ(τ)^{-1} − 1 on (V^{P_K})^∨, of the same dimension because a matrix and its transpose have equal rank.
acceptance: On wild invariants a tame generator acts by a matrix; inverse transpose has the same rank defect.

nodes.title: Unramified and tame character twists
nodes.statement: Let K be complete for a normalised discrete valuation with perfect residue field of characteristic p>0. Let F be a topological field of characteristic different from p, and V a finite-dimensional continuous F-representation of G_K with finite wild image. The arbitrary-perfect-residue-field case retains the recorded ramification-theory gap. An unramified character twist preserves a and Sw. A tame character twist preserves the positive breaks and Sw, but can change the tame Artin contribution.

nodes.title: Twisting by a character of larger break
nodes.statement: Let K be complete for a normalised discrete valuation with perfect residue field of characteristic p>0. Let F be a topological field of characteristic different from p, and V a finite-dimensional continuous F-representation of G_K with finite wild image. The arbitrary-perfect-residue-field case retains the recorded ramification-theory gap. If a continuous character χ has break u(χ)>0 strictly larger than every break of V, then every break of V⊗χ is u(χ), Sw(V⊗χ)=u(χ)dim V and a(V⊗χ)=a(χ)dim V.
hypotheses: Let K be complete for a normalised discrete valuation with perfect residue field of characteristic p>0. Let F be a topological field of characteristic different from p, and V a finite-dimensional continuous F-representation of G_K with finite wild image. The arbitrary-perfect-residue-field case retains the recorded ramification-theory gap.
proofSteps: (c): V ⊗ χ is the tensor product with the character (Mathlib Representation.tprod, R01.1/restriction-dual-tensor-twist), realised on V with σ acting by χ(σ)ρ(σ). Unramified χ is trivial on I_K; tame χ is trivial on G_K^u for u > 0; for u(χ) larger than the breaks of V, G_K^{u(χ)} acts trivially on V and by a nontrivial scalar on V ⊗ χ, while G_K^{u(χ)+} acts trivially on both (Ulmer 2016 §4, a(ρ ⊗ χ) = deg(ρ) a(χ)).
acceptance: Strictness matters: twisting χ by χ⁻¹ at equal breaks can cancel ramification.

nodes.title: Upper numbering of the subgroup G_L: the function ψ_{L/K} of a finite separable extension
nodes.statement: Local setting of R01.3. Let L/K be a finite separable extension inside K^sep, not necessarily Galois, with ramification index e, residue degree f and different exponent d(L/K). For a finite Galois extension M/K containing L put ψ_{L/K} := φ_{M/L} ∘ ψ_{M/K} on [−1, ∞), where φ and ψ are the Herbrand functions of the Galois extensions M/L and M/K (LocalFieldsRamification layer 3). Then: (a) ψ_{L/K} does not depend on M and is the Herbrand function ψ when L/K is Galois; it is continuous, strictly increasing and piecewise linear, ψ_{L/K}(u) = u for −1 ≤ u ≤ 0, and ψ_{M/K} = ψ_{M/L} ∘ ψ_{L/K} for every finite Galois M/K containing L; (b) G_K^u ∩ G_L = G_L^{ψ_{L/K}(u)} for every real u ≥ −1, where G_K^u and G_L^w are the absolute upper filtrations of R01.3/breaks-and-swan-conductor; (c) for u ≥ 0, ψ_{L/K}(u) = (1/f)·∫_0^u [G_K : G_K^t·G_L] dt; (d) for u larger than every break, ψ_{L/K}(u) = e·u − d(L/K) + e − 1, equivalently ∫_0^∞ ([L:K] − [G_K : G_K^t·G_L]) dt = f·(d(L/K) − e + 1) = δ(L/K) − [L:K] + f, with δ(L/K) = f·d(L/K) the discriminant exponent.
hypotheses: K as in the local setting of R01.3; tier (F) (finite residue field) is supplied by the LocalFieldsRamification layers cited; tier (P) rests on the gap 'Ramification filtration over a perfect infinite residue field'
L/K finite separable; no normality of L/K
the lower numbering of Gal(M/K) restricts to that of the subgroup Gal(M/L); the upper numbering does not, and ψ_{L/K} measures the difference
proofSteps: Independence of M and (a): for finite Galois M ⊆ M′ over K, both containing L, the tower formulas of LocalFieldsRamification layer 3 (herbrand_tower, inverseHerbrand_tower), applied to M′ ⊇ M ⊇ K and to M′ ⊇ M ⊇ L, where M/K and M/L are Galois, give ψ_{M′/K} = ψ_{M′/M} ∘ ψ_{M/K} and φ_{M′/L} = φ_{M/L} ∘ φ_{M′/M}; hence φ_{M′/L} ∘ ψ_{M′/K} = φ_{M/L} ∘ ψ_{M/K}, and two choices of M are compared inside their compositum. If L/K is Galois, φ_{M/K} = φ_{L/K} ∘ φ_{M/L} gives φ_{M/L} ∘ ψ_{M/K} = ψ_{L/K}. Continuity, monotonicity, piecewise linearity and the identity on [−1, 0] are inherited from φ_{M/L} and ψ_{M/K}; ψ_{M/L} ∘ ψ_{L/K} = ψ_{M/K} because ψ_{M/L} ∘ φ_{M/L} = id.

(b) at finite level: with G = Gal(M/K) and H = Gal(M/L), G^u ∩ H = G_{ψ_{M/K}(u)} ∩ H = H_{ψ_{M/K}(u)} (compatibility of the lower numbering, with real index, with subgroups) = H^{φ_{M/L}(ψ_{M/K}(u))} = H^{ψ_{L/K}(u)}.

(b) for the absolute groups: σ ∈ G_L lies in G_K^u iff σ|_M ∈ Gal(M/K)^u for every finite Galois M/K; those M containing L are cofinal, and every finite Galois M_1/L is contained in such an M, with Gal(M_1/L)^w the image of Gal(M/L)^w (upperRamificationGroup_quotient). So σ ∈ G_K^u iff σ|_M ∈ Gal(M/L)^{ψ_{L/K}(u)} for all such M, iff σ ∈ G_L^{ψ_{L/K}(u)}.

(c): [G_K : G_K^t·G_L] = [G : G^t·H] = [L:K]·|G^t ∩ H|/|G^t|. Where ψ_{M/K} is differentiable at t, the chain rule gives ψ′_{L/K}(t) = φ′_{M/L}(w)·ψ′_{M/K}(t) = (|H_w|/|H_0|)·(|G_0|/|G_w|) with w = ψ_{M/K}(t), which equals e·|G^t ∩ H|/|G^t| because |G_0|/|H_0| = e(M/K)/e(M/L) = e. Hence [G_K : G_K^t·G_L] = f·ψ′_{L/K}(t) outside the finitely many breaks, and (c) follows by integration from ψ_{L/K}(0) = 0.

(d): Hilbert's formula d(M/K) = Σ_{i≥0}(|G_i| − 1) gives φ_{M/K}(v) = (v + d(M/K) − e(M/K) + 1)/e(M/K) for v beyond the last lower break, that is ψ_{M/K}(u) = e(M/K)·u − d(M/K) + e(M/K) − 1 for u large, and likewise for M/L. Composing and using the tower formula d(M/K) = d(M/L) + e(M/L)·d(L/K) for the different exponent (LocalFieldsRamification layer 3) gives ψ_{L/K}(u) = e·u − d(L/K) + e − 1. By (c), ∫_0^U ([L:K] − [G_K : G_K^t·G_L]) dt = f·(e·U − ψ_{L/K}(U)) for every U.
acceptance: K = Q_3, L = Q_3(∛3) (not Galois; e = 3, f = 1, d(L/K) = 5): ψ_{L/K}(u) = u for 0 ≤ u ≤ 3/2 and 3u − 3 for u ≥ 3/2; the Galois closure Q_3(ζ_3, ∛3), with group S_3, has the single wild upper break 3/2 and different exponent 11 = 1 + 2·5; ∫_0^∞ (3 − [G_K : G_K^t·G_L]) dt = 2·(3/2) = 3 = f·(d − e + 1)
L/K tamely ramified of index e, Galois or not: ψ_{L/K}(u) = e·u for u ≥ 0 (d = e − 1), the tame base change of R01.3/conductor-unramified-base-change
L/K unramified: ψ_{L/K} = id and G_L^u = G_K^u ∩ G_L

nodes.title: Invariants of an induced representation
nodes.statement: Let Γ be profinite, H open, D closed normal, and U a continuous finite-dimensional representation of H. Then dim(Ind_H^ΓU)^D=[Γ:H·D]dimU^{H∩D}.
hypotheses: Let Γ be profinite, H open, D closed normal, and U a continuous finite-dimensional representation of H.
proofSteps: Mackey for the closed subgroup D (R01.1/mackey-decomposition): Res_D Ind_H^Γ U ≅ ⊕_{HsD} Ind_{D_s}^D (U^s|_{D_s}) with D_s = D ∩ s⁻¹Hs. Since D is normal, HsD = (H·D)s, so the double cosets are the [Γ : H·D] right cosets of the open subgroup H·D, and D_s = s⁻¹(D ∩ H)s.
Shapiro (R01.1/continuous-induction (c)): (Ind_{D_s}^D W)^D ≅ W^{D_s}; for W = U^s, on which y acts by σ(sys⁻¹), this is U^{sD_s s⁻¹} = U^{H ∩ D}. Summing over the double cosets gives the formula.

nodes.title: Induction preserves finite wild image
nodes.statement: Let Γ be profinite, H open, D closed normal, and U a continuous finite-dimensional representation of H. If V has finite wild image on G_L, then Ind_{G_L}^{G_K}V has finite wild image.
hypotheses: Let Γ be profinite, H open, D closed normal, and U a continuous finite-dimensional representation of H.
proofSteps: Finite wild image: N := P_L ∩ ker(ρ_V) is normal in G_L and of finite index in P_L = P_K ∩ G_L, hence in P_K; it has finitely many G_K-conjugates (its normaliser contains G_L), all inside P_K, so their intersection N′ is normal in G_K and of finite index in P_K. For n ∈ N′, f ∈ Ind V and x ∈ G_K, (n·f)(x) = f(xn) = f(xnx⁻¹·x) = ρ_V(xnx⁻¹)f(x) = f(x), so N′ acts trivially and P_K acts through the finite group P_K/N′.
acceptance: Use the finite intersection of conjugates of the wild-action kernel, rather than a finite quotient of all G_L.

nodes.title: The local induction formula for conductors, in rational form
nodes.statement: Local setting of R01.3. Let L/K be a finite separable extension inside K^sep with ramification index e, residue degree f, different exponent d(L/K) and discriminant exponent δ(L/K) = f·d(L/K) (LocalFieldsRamification layer 3), and let V be a continuous representation of G_L on a finite-dimensional vector space over a field F of characteristic ≠ p such that the image of P_L is finite. Then the image of P_K on Ind_{G_L}^{G_K} V (R01.1/continuous-induction) is finite and, as identities of rational numbers: (a) codim (Ind V)^{I_K} = ([L:K] − f)·dim V + f·codim V^{I_L}; (b) Sw_K(Ind V) = f·Sw_L(V) + (δ(L/K) − [L:K] + f)·dim V; (c) a_K(Ind_{G_L}^{G_K} V) = δ(L/K)·dim V + f·a_L(V). In particular a_K(Ind_{G_L}^{G_K} 1) = δ(L/K) (the conductor–discriminant formula) and Sw_K(Ind 1) = f·(d(L/K) − e + 1). Neither the integrality of conductors nor any global statement is used, and V need not factor through a finite quotient of G_L.
hypotheses: K as in the local setting of R01.3; tier (F) (finite residue field) is supplied by the LocalFieldsRamification layers cited; tier (P) rests on the gap 'Ramification filtration over a perfect infinite residue field'
L/K separable, not necessarily Galois; char F ≠ p and finite wild image of V
a and Sw are the rational numbers of R01.3/artin-conductor-with-its-wild-part and R01.3/breaks-and-swan-conductor; this node is upstream of R01.3/hasse-arf-integrality
proofSteps: Finite wild image and (a): R01.3/invariants-of-an-induced-representation with D = I_K gives dim (Ind V)^{I_K} = f·dim V^{I_L}, and dim Ind V = [L:K]·dim V.

For u > 0 the same lemma with D = G_K^u (closed and normal) gives dim (Ind V)^{G_K^u} = [G_K : G_K^u·G_L]·dim V^{G_K^u ∩ G_L}, and G_K^u ∩ G_L = G_L^{ψ_{L/K}(u)} (R01.3/upper-numbering-of-an-open-subgroup (b)).

nodes.title: Ramification break of an Artin–Schreier extension
nodes.statement: Let K have characteristic p>0, be complete for a normalised discrete valuation with perfect residue field, and let u∈K have v(u)=−m<0 with p∤m. Put L=K(α), α^p−α=u. L/K is cyclic of degree p, totally ramified, with unique lower and upper break m.
hypotheses: Let K have characteristic p>0, be complete for a normalised discrete valuation with perfect residue field, and let u∈K have v(u)=−m<0 with p∤m. Put L=K(α), α^p−α=u.
proofSteps: Extend v_K to L: p·v(α) = v(u) = −m because v(α) < 0, so v(α) = −m/p ∉ Z when p ∤ m; hence e(L/K) = p = [L:K], L/K is totally ramified, and it is Galois with group F_p since α + c (c ∈ F_p) are the roots.

Choose integers a, b with −m·a + p·b = 1 and put π_L = α^a π_K^b, a uniformiser; p ∤ a. For σ with σ(α) = α + c, c ∈ F_p^×: σ(π_L)/π_L − 1 = (1 + c/α)^a − 1 has valuation v_L(α^{-1}) = m, so v_L(σ(π_L) − π_L) = m + 1 and σ ∈ G_m \ G_{m+1} (LocalFieldsRamification layer 3 lower filtration).
acceptance: If p divides m, cancellation by changing α can lower the break and this computation cannot be used.

nodes.title: The conductor exponent of an elliptic curve
nodes.statement: Let K be as in R01.3/breaks-and-swan-conductor (perfect residue field of characteristic p, tier (F) or (P)), R = O_K, and E/K an elliptic curve given by a Weierstrass curve W over K with W.IsElliptic. For a prime ℓ ≠ p let V_ℓ E = T_ℓ E ⊗ Q_ℓ with its continuous G_K-action (R01.6/tate-module-of-an-abelian-variety, compared with EllipticCurves layer 2 by R01.6/elliptic-tate-module-comparison). Define f(E) := a(V_ℓ₀ E) with ℓ₀ the least prime different from p, ε(E) := codim (V_ℓ₀ E)^{I_K} and δ(E) := Sw(V_ℓ₀ E), so f(E) = ε(E) + δ(E). Theorem part: (i) for every prime ℓ ≠ p, a(V_ℓ E) = f(E), ε and δ are independent of ℓ, and δ(E) = Sw(E[ℓ]); (ii) ε(E) = 0, 1, 2 according as the minimal equation W.minimal R has good, multiplicative or additive reduction (Mathlib HasGoodReduction, HasMultiplicativeReduction, HasAdditiveReduction); (iii) δ(E) = 0 when p ≥ 5, and when E has good or multiplicative reduction; (iv) a(V_ℓ E^∨) = a(H¹) = f(E). For a number field F and E/F, N_E := ∏_v 𝔭_v^{f(E_{F_v})}, with exponent 0 exactly at the places of good reduction.
hypotheses: ℓ ≠ p (the residue characteristic, not the characteristic of K)
reduction types refer to the minimal equation W.minimal R, never to a bare integral equation
the canonical choice ℓ₀ makes the definition choice-free; independence of ℓ is a theorem
proofSteps: Independence of ℓ for ε: by (ii), proved case by case; the three reduction types of W.minimal R are exhaustive (WeierstrassCurve.hasGoodReduction_or_hasMultiplicativeReduction_or_hasAdditiveReduction). Good reduction ⇔ V_ℓ unramified is Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich (i) (EllipticCurves layer 4, ℓ ≠ p). Multiplicative: a curve with split multiplicative reduction is a Tate curve E_q (EllipticCurves layer 4), whose uniformisation gives 0 → Q_ℓ(1) → V → Q_ℓ → 0 with inertia acting through a nontrivial unipotent character, so dim V^{I} = 1 over every K of the local setting; a non-split one becomes split after an unramified quadratic twist (EllipticCurves layer 5), which changes V by an unramified character. Additive, potentially good: ρ(I_K) is finite (Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich (ii)) and nontrivial (i); if a nonzero vector were fixed by I_K then, det ρ = χ_ℓ being trivial on I_K, ρ(I_K) would be a finite group of unipotent matrices in characteristic 0, hence trivial; so V^{I} = 0. Additive, potentially multiplicative: V ≅ χ ⊗ V(Tate) with χ a ramified quadratic character (EllipticCurves layers 4–5), and an inertia element with χ = −1 has both eigenvalues −1, so V^{I} = 0.

Independence of ℓ for δ: δ(E) = Sw(E[ℓ]) for ℓ ≠ p by R01.3/reduction-does-not-increase-the-conductor (a); in the potentially good case the character of ρ(P_K) on V_ℓ is integer valued and independent of ℓ (traces of automorphisms α of the reduction: tr α = 1 + deg α − deg(1 − α), EllipticCurves layer 3), hence so is Sw; in the potentially multiplicative case δ = 2·Sw(χ) (Brumer–Kramer §6: each term is independent of ℓ; Serre 1970 n° 2.3, conjecture C3, stated to hold for abelian varieties at the end of n° 2.4).

(iii): for p ≥ 5 the inertia image in the potentially good case has order dividing 24, prime to p, so P_K acts trivially; χ quadratic is tame for p odd; good and multiplicative reduction have P_K acting trivially.
(iv): V_ℓ E^∨ ≅ V_ℓ E(−1) by the Weil pairing (R01.6), and twisting by the unramified χ_ℓ does not change a (R01.3/additivity-twist-and-unramified-invariance (c)).

nodes.title: Unramified descent of the Ogg invariants
nodes.statement: Let E/K be elliptic over the local perfect-residue-field setting, Δ_min its minimal Weierstrass discriminant, X its minimal proper regular model, and m the number of geometric irreducible components of X_k, without multiplicities. Passage to the completed strict henselisation preserves v(Δ_min), f(E), and m.
hypotheses: Let E/K be elliptic over the local perfect-residue-field setting, Δ_min its minimal Weierstrass discriminant, X its minimal proper regular model, and m the number of geometric irreducible components of X_k, without multiplicities.
proofSteps: Reduce to R strictly henselian with algebraically closed residue field, as the R11.2 nodes require: let R′ be the completion of the strict henselisation of R and K′ its fraction field (the completion of K^ur). (i) v(Δ_min) does not depend on the minimal equation chosen, two minimal equations being related by a change of variables (WeierstrassCurve.valuation_Δ_eq_of_isMinimal_smul); W stays minimal over R′ and v(Δ_min) is unchanged, and the ReductionSymbol is unchanged, because R → R′ is unramified (EllipticCurves layer 4). (ii) f(E) is unchanged (R01.3/conductor-unramified-base-change, tier (P)). (iii) X ⊗_R R′ is the minimal proper regular model of E over K′, with special fibre X_k ⊗_k k̄, so m is the same number (StableReduction layer 5: formation of the minimal regular model commutes with this base change). Over R′, R11.2/kodaira-geometric-configurations identifies the special fibre with the configuration of the ReductionSymbol, so m is the component count of the symbol: 1, n, 1, 2, 3, 5, n + 5, 7, 8, 9 for I_0, I_n, II, III, IV, I_0*, I_n*, IV*, III*, II*.
acceptance: For I₀* count five regular-model components, rather than four Néron components.

nodes.title: Ogg formula in residue characteristic at least five
nodes.statement: Let E/K be elliptic over the local perfect-residue-field setting, Δ_min its minimal Weierstrass discriminant, X its minimal proper regular model, and m the number of geometric irreducible components of X_k, without multiplicities. If p≥5, v(Δ_min)=f(E)+m−1.
hypotheses: Let E/K be elliptic over the local perfect-residue-field setting, Δ_min its minimal Weierstrass discriminant, X its minimal proper regular model, and m the number of geometric irreducible components of X_k, without multiplicities.
proofSteps: p ≥ 5 (direct): δ = 0 (R01.3/conductor-of-an-elliptic-curve (iii)), so f = ε; read v(Δ_min) and m off each ReductionSymbol (Tate's algorithm, EllipticCurves layer 4, whose output in residue characteristic ≥ 5 determines v(Δ_min) by the values below; component counts from R11.2/kodaira-geometric-configurations; R11.2/wild-kodaira-comparison records that these values of v(Δ_min) are not valid in residue characteristics 2 and 3): I_0: 0 = 0 + 1 − 1; I_n: n = 1 + n − 1; II: 2 = 2 + 1 − 1; III: 3 = 2 + 2 − 1; IV: 4 = 2 + 3 − 1; I_0*: 6 = 2 + 5 − 1; I_n*: n + 6 = 2 + (n + 5) − 1; IV*: 8 = 2 + 7 − 1; III*: 9 = 2 + 8 − 1; II*: 10 = 2 + 9 − 1.
acceptance: For I₀* the calculation is 6=2+5−1; the tame discriminant table cannot be used at 2 or 3.

nodes.title: Ogg conductor formula in every residue characteristic
nodes.statement: Let E/K be elliptic over the local perfect-residue-field setting, Δ_min its minimal Weierstrass discriminant, X its minimal proper regular model, and m the number of geometric irreducible components of X_k, without multiplicities. In every residue characteristic, including two and three in mixed and equal characteristic, v(Δ_min)=f(E)+m−1.
hypotheses: Let E/K be elliptic over the local perfect-residue-field setting, Δ_min its minimal Weierstrass discriminant, X its minimal proper regular model, and m the number of geometric irreducible components of X_k, without multiplicities.
proofSteps: All p (uniform): apply R01.3/saito-conductor-discriminant to the minimal regular model: −Art(X/S) = ord Δ_{X/S}, with ord Δ_{X/S} = v(Δ_min) and −Art(X/S) = f(E) + m − 1 (χ(X_K̄) = 0, χ(X_k̄) = m − 1 + ε(E), Swan term δ(E)) (Saito 1988 Cor. 2 as stated by Liu 1994 and Brumer–Kramer §6; DDT §2.2: Ogg's formula, proved by Saito for p = 2).
acceptance: The all-characteristics route retains the Saito input gap; Ogg’s original wild case analysis is not asserted as read.

nodes.title: Saito conductor–discriminant theorem
nodes.statement: Let R be a complete DVR with perfect residue field of characteristic p, K its fraction field, C/K a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus at least one, and X/R its minimal regular model. With Art(X/R)=χ(X_K̄)−χ(X_k̄)−Sw(H¹_et(C_K̄,Q_ℓ)), ℓ≠p, and Deligne’s discriminant Δ_{X/R}, one has −Art(X/R)=ordΔ_{X/R}, in the generality quoted in Liu 1994.
hypotheses: Let R be a complete DVR with perfect residue field of characteristic p, K its fraction field, C/K a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus at least one, and X/R its minimal regular model.
proofSteps: Liu 1994, Introduction, quotes this as Saito 1988 Theorem 1. The original was not obtainable; its exact hypotheses and proof remain unverifiable. The cohomological Artin-conductor definition, Deligne discriminant and comparison theorem are the recorded gap, not consequences of the Galois conductor formulas.
acceptance: No stronger scope than Liu’s quoted minimal-regular-model theorem is asserted.

nodes.title: Genus-one comparison of discriminants and Euler characteristics
nodes.statement: Let R be a complete DVR with perfect residue field of characteristic p, K its fraction field, C/K a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus at least one, and X/R its minimal regular model. For C=E elliptic, ordΔ_{X/R}=v(Δ_min) and χ(X_k̄)=m−1+ε(E), whereas χ(X_K̄)=0. Consequently −Art(X/R)=f(E)+m−1.
hypotheses: Let R be a complete DVR with perfect residue field of characteristic p, K its fraction field, C/K a smooth projective geometrically connected curve of genus at least one, and X/R its minimal regular model.
proofSteps: Genus one: Deligne's discriminant of the minimal regular model is the minimal Weierstrass discriminant; the special fibre of the minimal regular model has b_0 = 1, b_2 = m and b_1 = dim V^{I_K} = 2 − ε(E) (the specialisation identity b_1(X_k̄) = dim H¹(X_K̄, Q_ℓ)^{I_K}, part (1) of the recorded gap; R11.2/minimal-regular-smooth-locus identifies the smooth locus of X with the Néron model over a strictly henselian base and does not state this identity), giving χ(X_k̄) = m − 1 + ε.

Statement as read: Liu 1994 recalls Art(X/S) and ord Δ = −Art(X/S) ([Sa1] Theorem 1) and Ogg's formula ([Sa1] Cor. 2); Brumer–Kramer §6 and DDT §2.2 attribute the residue-characteristic-2 case of Ogg's formula to Saito.
acceptance: The fibre-specialisation identity for H¹ remains part of the Saito input gap.

nodes.title: Serre's bound for the wild invariant of a representation of a p-adic Galois group
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, complete for a discrete valuation with perfect residue field of characteristic p > 0, with absolute ramification index e_K = v_K(p). Let V be a vector space of finite dimension N over a field F of characteristic ≠ p and ρ: G_K → GL_F(V) a continuous homomorphism with finite image G = Gal(L/K), with ramification groups G_i of orders g_i, and let p^c = g_1 be the order of the wild inertia group. Then Sw(V) ≤ N·e_K·(c + 1/(p − 1)) and a(V) ≤ N·(1 + e_K·c + e_K/(p − 1)) (Serre 1987, Proposition 9 and its corollary (4.9.4), where Sw(V) is written b(ρ) and a(V) is written n(ρ)). Serre's statement adds that both inequalities are strict when G_1 is not cyclic; that refinement rests on Serre, Local Fields IV §2, Exercise 3, and is not part of this node.
hypotheses: char K = 0 (e_K is finite); char F ≠ p; ρ(G_K) finite

Hilbert's formula and Hensel's bound for the different: tier (F) (finite residue field) is supplied by the LocalFieldsRamification layers cited; tier (P) rests on the gap 'Ramification filtration over a perfect infinite residue field'
the strict inequality for non-cyclic G_1 is deliberately left out: its proof was not read
proofSteps: Let I be the largest index with G_I ≠ 1 (if G_1 = 1 then Sw(V) = 0). Since codim V^{G_i} ≤ N for 1 ≤ i ≤ I and = 0 for i > I, the lower-numbering sum of R01.3/breaks-and-swan-conductor gives Sw(V) ≤ (N/g_0)·(g_1 + … + g_I) = (N/g_0)·(I + Σ_{i≥1}(g_i − 1)) (Serre (4.9.5)).

Different: let L_0 = L ∩ K^ur, so that L/L_0 is totally ramified with group G_0 and v_L(p) = g_0·e_K. Hilbert's formula and Hensel's bound (LocalFieldsRamification layer 3) give Σ_{i≥0}(g_i − 1) = d(L/L_0) ≤ g_0 − 1 + v_L(g_0) = g_0 − 1 + c·g_0·e_K, the prime-to-p part of g_0 being a unit; hence Σ_{i≥1}(g_i − 1) ≤ g_0·e_K·c (Serre (4.9.7)).

Last break: I ≤ g_0·e_K/(p − 1) (Serre (4.9.6)), proved from the same inputs: if I ≥ 1 take τ ∈ G_I of order p and L′ the fixed field of ⟨τ⟩; L/L′ is cyclic of degree p and totally ramified, with ramification groups ⟨τ⟩ ∩ G_i (compatibility of the lower numbering with subgroups), so its unique break is I and d(L/L′) = (p − 1)(I + 1); Hensel's bound for L/L′ gives (p − 1)(I + 1) ≤ p − 1 + v_L(p) = p − 1 + g_0·e_K.
Combine: Sw(V) ≤ (N/g_0)·(g_0·e_K/(p − 1) + g_0·e_K·c) = N·e_K·(c + 1/(p − 1)), and a(V) = codim V^{G_0} + Sw(V) ≤ N + Sw(V) (R01.3/artin-conductor-with-its-wild-part).
acceptance: p = 3, K = Q_3, V = E[2] for an elliptic curve E (N = 2; G_1 lies in a 3-Sylow subgroup of GL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3, so c ≤ 1): a(V) ≤ 2·(1 + 1 + 1/2) = 5 (Serre §4.9 (a))
p = 2, K = Q_2, V = E[3] (N = 2; G_1 lies in the quaternion group of order 8, c ≤ 3): a(V) ≤ 2·(1 + 3 + 1) = 10; Serre's strict form gives 9, and 8 needs a finer analysis (§4.9 (b))
Equality: χ_8 over Q_2 (N = 1, c = 1, e_K = 1): Sw = 2 = 1·1·(1 + 1), with G_1 cyclic

sources.match: Serre's Proposition 9: with p^c the order of the wild inertia group G_1 and N = dim V, b(ρ) ≤ N·e_K·(c + 1/(p − 1)), strict if G_1 is not cyclic (the text layer prints p^c as 'pC' and ≤ as <). The node states the non-strict form.

The proof: d = Σ(g_i − 1) is the valuation of the different, bounded by Hensel's inequality d ≤ g_0 − 1 + g_0·e_K·c; (4.9.6) is quoted from Local Fields p. 79, Exercise 3, and is reproved here in its non-strict form from Hensel's bound.

nodes.title: Global residual elliptic conductor
nodes.statement: Let E/Q be elliptic and ℓ≥5 prime. Write E[ℓ] for the actual continuous residual representation on its geometric ℓ-torsion, without semisimplification. Then N(E[ℓ])=N_E^{(ℓ)}/∏_{q∥N_E,q≠ℓ,ℓ|v_q(Δ_min)}q. Thus N(E[ℓ]) divides N_E. For the globally semisimplified residual representation only N(E[ℓ]ˢˢ)∣N(E[ℓ]) is asserted without further irreducibility hypotheses.
hypotheses: Let E/K be elliptic over a nonarchimedean local field of residue characteristic p, and ℓ≠p prime. E[ℓ] is the reduction of T_ℓE; its Swan conductor equals δ(E).

For global semisimplification restrict a global composition series to each inertia group and apply R01.3/additivity-twist-and-unramified-invariance; it gives the divisibility inequality, not equality.

nodes.title: Complex conjugations and odd rank-two representations
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, F̄ an algebraic closure and G_F = Field.absoluteGaloisGroup F with its Krull topology. (1) Complex conjugations. For a real infinite place v of F (NumberField.InfinitePlace.IsReal) and a field embedding ι : F̄ → ℂ whose restriction to F is a real embedding inducing v, the image ι(F̄) is stable under complex conjugation conj = Complex.conjAe, and c_ι := ι⁻¹ ∘ conj ∘ ι ∈ G_F. Then c_ι² = 1, c_ι ≠ 1, and for two such embeddings ι, ι′ above the same v the elements c_ι, c_ι′ are conjugate in G_F; write c_v for this conjugacy class. (2) Totally odd characters. A continuous character μ : G_F → A^× with values in a topological commutative ring A is totally odd if μ(c_v) = −1 for every real place v of F (the condition does not depend on the choice of c_v in its class). (3) Odd representations. Let A be a topological commutative ring and ρ ∈ ContinuousRep G_F A M with M finite projective of rank 2 over A (R01.1/continuous-representation). ρ is odd at the real place v if det_A ρ(c_v) = −1 in A, and odd (totally odd) if it is odd at every real place of F, i.e. if det ρ is totally odd. For F = ℚ there is exactly one real place and c is any complex conjugation. When F has no real place every ρ is odd. Pinned conventions: (a) oddness depends only on the character det ρ; (b) if A is a field of characteristic ≠ 2, ρ is odd at v iff Tr ρ(c_v) = 0 iff ρ(c_v) is conjugate to diag(1, −1); (c) if A is a reduced ring in which 2 = 0 (for instance A = k a field of characteristic 2) then u = det ρ(c_v) satisfies u² = 1, so (u − 1)² = 0, u = 1 = −1, and every rank-two ρ is odd; for a non-reduced A with 2 = 0 this fails (over the dual numbers A = F_2[ε]/(ε²) the character μ : G_ℚ → Gal(ℚ(i)/ℚ) → {1, 1 + ε} ⊂ A^× has μ(c) = 1 + ε ≠ −1, so μ ⊕ 1 is not odd); the condition ‘ρ(c_v) ≠ 1’ used in characteristic two is a separate condition, named non-trivial at v, and is never part of oddness.
hypotheses: F is a number field; G_F carries the Krull topology
A is a topological commutative ring and M a finite projective A-module of rank 2 (free of rank 2 in framed coordinates)
c_v is well defined only up to conjugacy in G_F; every statement is conjugation invariant
over a reduced ring with 2 = 0 (in particular a field of characteristic two) oddness is automatic; over a non-reduced ring with 2 = 0 it is a genuine condition; ρ(c) ≠ 1 is a separate hypothesis
proofSteps: Since ι|_F lands in ℝ (mathlib:NumberField.ComplexEmbedding.IsReal for the embedding ι|_F, mathlib:NumberField.InfinitePlace.IsReal for the place v it induces), conj fixes ι(F) and preserves the algebraic closure ι(F̄) of ι(F) in ℂ, so c_ι is an F-automorphism of F̄; c_ι² = 1 because conj² = 1, and c_ι ≠ 1 because F̄ is not contained in ℝ (it contains √−1).

Two embeddings above v differ by an element g ∈ G_F (both restrict on F to the unique real embedding σ_v inducing v and both have image the algebraic closure of σ_v(F) in ℂ, so g := ι⁻¹ ∘ ι′ is an F-automorphism of F̄ and ι′ = ι ∘ g), so c_ι′ = g⁻¹ c_ι g.

det ρ is a continuous character G_F → A^× (the determinant of R01.1/continuous-representation: the action on the top exterior power of a finite projective module of constant rank 2; when M is free it is mathlib:LinearMap.det ∘ ρ, and for a framed representation mathlib:Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup.det of the matrix. LinearMap.det by itself is not the definition: for a projective module without a finite basis Mathlib gives it the value 1), so det ρ(c_v) is well defined on the class c_v; oddness of ρ is total oddness of det ρ.

If A is a field with char A ≠ 2, ρ(c_v)² = 1 forces ρ(c_v) to be diagonalisable with eigenvalues in {±1}; the determinant is −1 exactly when the eigenvalues are 1 and −1, exactly when the trace is 0 (traces of ±1 are ±2 ≠ 0).

Serre 1987, 1.3 (1.3.8), printed p. 182, fixes the convention det ρ(c) = −1 for G_ℚ and records that it is automatic for p = 2 and means ρ(c) ∼ diag(1, −1) for p ≠ 2; Khare–Wintenberger I §1 define S-type with ‘det ρ̄(c) = −1 for c a complex conjugation’.
acceptance: For p odd and χ̄_p : G_ℚ → F_p^× the mod-p cyclotomic character (mathlib:modularCyclotomicCharacter for L = ℚ̄ and n = p, which asks for the count Nat.card (rootsOfUnity p ℚ̄) = p), χ̄_p ⊕ 1 is odd since c acts on μ_p by inversion; any ρ̄ with det ρ̄ = χ̄_p is odd (the case of E[p], R01.6/determinant-and-oddness).
Over F_5, ρ = χ_{−3} ⊕ χ_{−4} (quadratic characters of ℚ(√−3), ℚ(i)) has ρ(c) = −1 ≠ 1 but det ρ(c) = 1, so it is not odd: ‘ρ(c) ≠ 1’ is not oddness.

In characteristic two the trivial representation of G_ℚ on F_2² is odd but not non-trivial at c; the representation of G_ℚ on E[2] for E : y² = x³ − 2 is odd and non-trivial at c (c is a transposition of the three roots of x³ − 2).

Then χ(c_{v₊}) = 1 (the field F(√(√2)) = ℚ(2^{1/4}) is real above v₊) and χ(c_{v₋}) = −1 (√(−√2) is not real), so ρ = χ ⊕ 1 is odd at v₋, not odd at v₊, and not odd. api.name: TauCeti.GaloisRep.isConj_complexConjugation
api.statement: For every embedding ι : F̄ → ℂ above the real place v, the element c_ι = ι⁻¹ ∘ conj ∘ ι (the σ ∈ G_F with ι(σx) = conj(ι(x)) for all x) is conjugate in G_F to the chosen c_v; hence two complex conjugations above the same real place are conjugate in G_F.

api.name: TauCeti.GaloisRep.IsTotallyOddChar
api.statement: A continuous character μ : G_F → A^× is totally odd iff μ(c_v) = −1 for every real place v.

api.statement: ρ is odd at v iff det ρ(c_v) = −1; IsOdd ρ iff IsOddAt ρ v for all real v, iff IsTotallyOddChar (det ρ).

api.name: TauCeti.GaloisRep.isOdd_tensor_character
api.statement: ρ ⊗ ψ is odd iff ρ is odd, for any continuous character ψ (det(ρ ⊗ ψ)(c) = det ρ(c) ψ(c)² and ψ(c)² = 1).

api.name: TauCeti.GaloisRep.isOdd_baseChange
api.statement: If ρ is odd then ρ ⊗_A B is odd for every continuous ring map A → B; the converse holds when A → B is injective, and also when det ρ(c_v) ∈ {1, −1} for every real v (automatic if A is a domain, or a local ring in which 2 is a unit) and 2 ≠ 0 in B. It fails in general: for A = k × k → B = k the second projection (char k ≠ 2) and det ρ(c) = (1, −1), ρ ⊗_A B is odd and ρ is not.

api.name: TauCeti.GaloisRep.isOdd_restrict

api.name: TauCeti.GaloisRep.isOdd_iff_conj_diag

nodes.title: Stable lines from a split nonscalar element
nodes.statement: Let k be a field and ρ:Γ→GL₂(k) a representation. If ρ(Γ) contains a nonscalar element whose characteristic polynomial splits over k, every ρ-stable line after arbitrary field extension is defined over k. Hence irreducibility is equivalent to absolute irreducibility.
hypotheses: Let k be a field and ρ:Γ→GL₂(k) a representation.
proofSteps: (a) If g is non-scalar with split characteristic polynomial, either g has two distinct eigenvalues in k (exactly two invariant lines over k′, both k-rational) or one eigenvalue λ ∈ k with g − λ nilpotent of rank 1 (exactly one invariant line ker(g − λ), k-rational). A ρ(Γ)-stable line of k′² is g-stable, hence one of these, hence k-rational and already ρ(Γ)-stable over k.
acceptance: A split rank-one Jordan block has a unique invariant line over k, even if k is imperfect.

nodes.title: Odd irreducible representations in odd characteristic
nodes.statement: Let k be a field and ρ:Γ→GL₂(k) a representation. For Γ=G_F, F with a real place v and char k≠2, if ρ is odd at v and irreducible over k, it is absolutely irreducible.
hypotheses: Let k be a field and ρ:Γ→GL₂(k) a representation.
proofSteps: (b) det ρ̄(c_v) = −1 and ρ̄(c_v)² = 1 give eigenvalues 1 and −1, distinct since char k ≠ 2, so g = ρ̄(c_v) satisfies (a). This is Serre 1987, 3.3 (b′). Serre argues from a decomposition of ρ ⊗ F̄_p into a direct sum of two lines; this is the only way in which a ρ irreducible over F_p can fail to be absolutely irreducible, because an irreducible representation over a perfect field stays semisimple after extension of scalars (directly: Gal(F̄_p/F_p) permutes the stable lines of F̄_p²; a stable line that is not F_p-rational has a second, distinct conjugate, and the two span; a unique stable line would be Galois-fixed, hence F_p-rational). Statement (a) reaches the same conclusion without this input and over any field k, perfect or not.
acceptance: Complex conjugation has the distinct eigenvalues one and minus one.

nodes.title: Dickson classification of finite projective images
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, k̄=F̄_p, and π:GL₂(k̄)→PGL₂(k̄). Finite-field subgroups are regarded inside k̄. Every finite H⊂PGL₂(k̄) fixes a point, is conjugate to PSL₂(F_q) or PGL₂(F_q), or is isomorphic to a dihedral group of order 2n with p∤n, n≥2, or A₄,S₄,A₅. These alternatives overlap; p can divide the exceptional group orders.
hypotheses: Let p be prime, k̄=F̄_p, and π:GL₂(k̄)→PGL₂(k̄). Finite-field subgroups are regarded inside k̄.
proofSteps: (a) A finite H ⊂ PGL_2(k̄) = PSL_2(k̄) is the image of a finite subgroup of SL_2(k̄), whose entries lie in a finite field F_s; so H ⊂ PSL_2(F_s), and Dickson 1901, Chapter XII (summary §260, pp. 285–286) applies; DDT Theorem 2.47(b) is the form used by the consumers. If p ∤ |H|: H is cyclic, dihedral of order 2n with p ∤ n, A_4, S_4 or A_5 by R01.4/finite-subgroups-of-pgl2-of-order-prime-to-the-characteristic (Dickson §§256–257); a cyclic H fixes a point of P¹(k̄). If p | |H|: by R01.4/subgroups-of-psl2-with-several-sylow-p-subgroups (Dickson §§251–254), either H has a single Sylow p-subgroup and fixes a point, (i); or, after conjugation in PGL_2(F_s), H is PSL_2(F_{p^m}) or PGL_2(F_{p^m}), (ii); or p^m = 2 and H is dihedral of order 2(1 + 2f) with 1 + 2f odd; or p = 3 and H ≅ A_5; the last two belong to (iii); every other H with p | |H| satisfies (i) or (ii) (among the groups isomorphic to A_4, S_4, A_5 these are: A_4 for p = 2, which fixes a point; A_4 ≅ PSL_2(F_3) and S_4 ≅ PGL_2(F_3) for p = 3; A_5 ≅ PSL_2(F_4) for p = 2 and A_5 ≅ PSL_2(F_5) for p = 5). Conjugacy: a subgroup of PGL_2(k̄) abstractly isomorphic to PSL_2(F_q) or PGL_2(F_q), q = p^r ≥ 4, has order divisible by p and more than one Sylow p-subgroup and is neither of the two exceptional kinds (its order is not twice an odd number, and for p = 3 it is not 60), so it is conjugate to PSL_2(F_{p^m}) or PGL_2(F_{p^m}), and comparing orders gives p^m = q and the type (Dickson §255 counts these conjugates inside PSL_2(F_s), and his footnote on p. 286 notes that for p = 2 and p = 5 the icosahedral subgroups are PSL_2(F_4) and PSL_2(F_5); §259: the icosahedral subgroups are all conjugate under PGL_2(F_s)).
acceptance: At p=3 the A₅ subgroup of PSL₂(F₉) must be retained; dyadic odd dihedral groups are retained.

nodes.title: Conjugacy of standard projective images
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, k̄=F̄_p, and π:GL₂(k̄)→PGL₂(k̄). Finite-field subgroups are regarded inside k̄. For q=p^r≥4, subgroups isomorphic to PSL₂(F_q), respectively PGL₂(F_q), form one conjugacy class in PGL₂(k̄). In characteristics two and five, A₅ is conjugate to PSL₂(F₄), respectively PSL₂(F₅).
hypotheses: Let p be prime, k̄=F̄_p, and π:GL₂(k̄)→PGL₂(k̄). Finite-field subgroups are regarded inside k̄.
proofSteps: Apply the multiple-Sylow classification in R01.4/subgroups-of-psl2-with-several-sylow-p-subgroups. Such an abstract group has multiple Sylow p-subgroups and cannot be an exceptional odd-dihedral group; in characteristic three its order is not sixty. The standard groups’ order formulas determine q and the type. The A₅ cases at two and five have the corresponding standard type.
acceptance: The characteristic-three A₅ case is exceptional, and is not claimed to be PSL₂ of a field of characteristic three.

nodes.title: Projective image and its coefficient field
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, k̄=F̄_p, and π:GL₂(k̄)→PGL₂(k̄). Finite-field subgroups are regarded inside k̄. If G⊂GL₂(k), k finite, acts absolutely irreducibly on k̄², its projective image is noncyclic, fixes no point, and is dihedral, exceptional, or conjugate to PSL₂(F₀) or PGL₂(F₀). In the last case F₀⊂k is generated by tr(g)²/det(g), g∈G.
hypotheses: Let p be prime, k̄=F̄_p, and π:GL₂(k̄)→PGL₂(k̄). Finite-field subgroups are regarded inside k̄.
proofSteps: (b) A cyclic π(G) makes G abelian (a central extension of a cyclic group), so G has a common eigenvector over k̄ (tauceti:TauCeti.exists_unitHom_jointEigenvector_of_pairwise_commute_of_isAlgClosed), contradicting absolute irreducibility; a fixed point of π(G) is a G-stable line. The function g ↦ Tr(g)²/det(g) is a class function on PGL_2, so its values on π(G) ⊂ PGL_2(k) lie in k; on PSL_2(F_0) it takes every square of F_0 (companion matrices), and the squares of F_0 generate F_0, so F_0 ⊂ k.
acceptance: Irreducibility only over k allows a nonsplit Cartan with cyclic projective image.

nodes.title: Linear image over the projective trace field
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, k̄=F̄_p, and π:GL₂(k̄)→PGL₂(k̄). Finite-field subgroups are regarded inside k̄. Let G⊂GL₂(k̄) be finite. If the projective image of G is conjugate to PSL₂(F₀) or PGL₂(F₀), #F₀≥4, then after conjugation [G,G]=SL₂(F₀) and G⊂k̄ˣ·GL₂(F₀). Conversely containment of SL₂(F₁), #F₁≥4, forces a standard projective image over F₀⊃F₁.
hypotheses: Let p be prime, k̄=F̄_p, and π:GL₂(k̄)→PGL₂(k̄). Finite-field subgroups are regarded inside k̄.
proofSteps: (c) Scalars are central, so [λA, μB] = [A, B] and [G, G] ⊂ [GL_2(F_0), GL_2(F_0)] = SL_2(F_0); [G, G] maps onto [π(G), π(G)] ⊇ PSL_2(F_0) (perfect, mathlib:SL2Simple.PSL_commutator_eq_top, whose hypothesis ∃ a ≠ 0, a² ≠ 1 follows from |F_0| ≥ 4 because at most three elements satisfy a = 0 or a² = 1), so [G,G]·{±1} = SL_2(F_0), and perfectness of SL_2(F_0) (mathlib:Matrix.SL2.commutator_eq_top) gives [G,G] = SL_2(F_0). Conversely PSL_2(F_1) ⊂ π(G) is non-solvable (mathlib:Group.IsPerfect.not_isSolvable), so π(G) is not Borel, dihedral, A_4, S_4; if π(G) ≅ A_5 then π(G) = PSL_2(F_1) with |F_1| ∈ {4, 5}; otherwise (a)(ii), and F_0 ⊃ F_1 by the trace-field argument of (b). [GL_2(F_0), GL_2(F_0)] = SL_2(F_0) and PGL_2(F_0)^{ab} = F_0^×/F_0^{×2} via det are R01.4/normal-subgroups-and-automorphisms-of-psl2-pgl2 (a); the non-solvability of SL_2(F_1) for |F_1| ≥ 4 is also tauceti:TauCeti.Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup.not_isSolvable_fin_two.
acceptance: The size condition excludes the nonperfect small special linear groups.

nodes.title: Dyadic solvable irreducible image
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, k̄=F̄_p, and π:GL₂(k̄)→PGL₂(k̄). Finite-field subgroups are regarded inside k̄. For p=2 a finite irreducible solvable G⊂GL₂(k̄) has dihedral projective image of order 2n with n odd at least three.

proofSteps: Apply R01.4/dickson-classification-and-the-dyadic-refinement. A₄ has a normal unipotent Klein subgroup, which forces a stable line; S₄ has an element of order four, impossible in GL₂(k̄) at two. A standard group of size at least four is nonsolvable; the remaining small standard group is S₃. The dihedral rotation order is odd in the dyadic case.

nodes.title: Large-order projective image criterion
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, k̄=F̄_p, and π:GL₂(k̄)→PGL₂(k̄). Finite-field subgroups are regarded inside k̄. Let G⊂GL₂(k̄) be finite. For absolutely irreducible G⊂GL₂(k̄), an element of projective order greater than five excludes A₄,S₄,A₅. Under this order hypothesis, if G is solvable its projective image is dihedral. Under the same hypothesis, if G is outside every torus normaliser, it contains a conjugate of SL₂(F_p).
hypotheses: Let p be prime, k̄=F̄_p, and π:GL₂(k̄)→PGL₂(k̄). Finite-field subgroups are regarded inside k̄.
proofSteps: (e) A_4, S_4, A_5 have no element of order > 5 (R01.4/finite-subgroups-of-pgl2-of-order-prime-to-the-characteristic, end of the statement; Serre 1972 Prop. 16); by (b) an absolutely irreducible G has π(G) dihedral, exceptional or of type (ii), and the solvable groups of type (ii) are PGL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3 (dihedral), PSL_2(F_3) ≅ A_4 and PGL_2(F_3) ≅ S_4, so a solvable G with an element of order > 5 in π(G) has dihedral image; a dihedral image of order 2n (p ∤ n) puts G in the normaliser of the maximal torus of GL_2(k̄) that contains the preimage of a cyclic subgroup of index 2; in the last case (a) therefore leaves PSL_2/PGL_2(F_{p^a}) with p^a ≥ 4, and (c) gives a conjugate of SL_2(F_{p^a}) ⊃ SL_2(F_p) inside G.
acceptance: A nonsplit Cartan over F_q is irreducible over F_q and solvable with projective order q+1, so absolute irreducibility is essential.

nodes.title: Prime-field subgroups with elements of order ell
nodes.statement: Let ℓ be prime, V a two-dimensional F_ℓ-space and G⊂GL(V). If ℓ divides #G, then G contains SL(V) or lies in a Borel subgroup.
hypotheses: Let ℓ be prime, V a two-dimensional F_ℓ-space and G⊂GL(V).
proofSteps: (a) Serre's proof: ℓ | |G| gives an element of order ℓ (Cauchy, mathlib:exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card'); it generates an ℓ-group (mathlib:IsPGroup), hence is a transvection fixing a unique line (R01.4/p-subgroups-and-borel-subgroups). If all these lines coincide, G stabilises the common line, i.e. lies in a Borel subgroup (in a basis beginning with a vector of the line every element of G has lower-left entry 0, tauceti:TauCeti.GL2Borel.mem_iff). Otherwise take two distinct such lines as coordinate axes: G contains [[1, a], [0, 1]] and [[1, 0], [b, 1]] with ab ≠ 0, and these generate SL_2(F_ℓ) by R01.4/two-transvections-generate-sl2-over-a-prime-field (Serre cites Bourbaki A III p. 104 prop. 17).
acceptance: Two distinct transvection lines generate SL₂ only with the prime-field hypothesis used here.

nodes.title: Cartan subgroups of GL_2 over a finite field and their normalisers
nodes.statement: Let k be a finite field with q elements, V a two-dimensional k-vector space and GL(V) ≅ GL_2(k). (1) Split Cartan: for two distinct lines D_1 ≠ D_2 of V, C_s(D_1, D_2) := {s ∈ GL(V) : sD_1 = D_1, sD_2 = D_2} ≅ (k^×)², the diagonal torus in a basis adapted to D_1 ⊕ D_2. (2) Non-split Cartan: for a subalgebra k′ ⊂ End_k(V) which is a field with q² elements, C_ns(k′) := k′^× ⊂ GL(V), cyclic of order q² − 1; in coordinates it is TauCeti.GL2NonSplitTorus k k′ hE, where k′ is taken as a field extension of k and hE : Module.finrank k k′ = 2 (left multiplication on k′ in the basis TauCeti.nonSplitTorusBasis k k′ hE); for q odd and ε ∈ k^× a non-square it is conjugate to {[[a, εb], [b, a]] : (a, b) ≠ (0, 0)}. (3) Normalisers: N(C) := normaliser of C in GL(V). For a split Cartan with q ≥ 3, N(C) is the stabiliser of the pair {D_1, D_2} (for q = 2, C is trivial and N(C) = GL(V)); for a non-split Cartan, N(C) consists of the k′-linear automorphisms of V (the elements of C) and the k′-semilinear ones, s(ax) = a^q s(x) for a ∈ k′, x ∈ V (the elements of N(C) ∖ C). If C is non-split, or split with q ≥ 3, then [N(C) : C] = 2, every element of N(C) ∖ C has trace 0 and square scalar, and the images C̄ ⊂ N̄ in PGL(V) are cyclic of order q ∓ 1 (− split, + non-split) and dihedral of order 2(q ∓ 1). (4) Borel: B(D) := stabiliser of a line D, of order q(q − 1)², TauCeti.GL2Borel k for D = ⟨e_1⟩. Half-Cartan (Serre): the subgroup of C_s(D_1, D_2) acting trivially on D_2.
hypotheses: k finite with q = |k| elements; q ≥ 3 for statements about split normalisers (for q = 2 the split Cartan is trivial)
Cartan subgroups are defined basis-free; matrix models are API
over F̄_p (consumers using algebraically closed coefficients) the image of a finite subgroup of a Cartan of GL_2(k) is diagonalisable over k̄
proofSteps: k′ = k[C] is a commutative semisimple k-algebra of rank 2 with C = k′^× (split: k × k; non-split: F_{q²}); an element of N(C) induces a k-algebra automorphism of k′, trivial exactly on C, and Aut_k(k′) has order 2 (swap, resp. Frobenius), so [N(C) : C] = 2 (Serre 1972 §2.2).

For s ∈ N(C) ∖ C, s² ∈ C commutes with s and is fixed by the swap/Frobenius, so s² ∈ k^× (scalar) and the characteristic polynomial is X² − s², trace 0 (split: s is antidiagonal; non-split: s(x) = λ x^q, s² = N(λ)).

By tauceti:TauCeti.exists_isConj_normalForm every element of GL_2(k) is a scalar, or conjugate to diag(a, b) with a ≠ b, or to a Jordan block, or to an element of the non-split torus outside k. Hence the union of the Cartan subgroups is the set of semisimple (order prime to p) elements; for p ≠ 2 an element with Tr² − 4 det ≠ 0 lies in exactly one Cartan, split iff Tr² − 4det is a square (Serre 1972 §2.1).

What the library has and what the node adds. Tau Ceti has: the non-split torus TauCeti.GL2NonSplitTorus F E hE of a degree-2 field extension E/F (any field F) in the basis TauCeti.nonSplitTorusBasis, its order q² − 1 (GL2NonSplitTorus.natCard_eq) and index q(q − 1) (tauceti:TauCeti.GL2NonSplitTorus.index_eq), the fact that a non-scalar element of it has no conjugate in the Borel subgroup (conj_notMem_gl2Borel) and that its centraliser is the torus (centralizer_gl2NonSplitTorusHom); the diagonal torus tauceti:TauCeti.diagonalTorus, range of TauCeti.diagGL, the centraliser of diag(t_0, t_1), t_0 ≠ t_1 (tauceti:TauCeti.centralizer_diagGL), the Weyl element tauceti:TauCeti.GL2WeylElement, which normalises the diagonal torus (gl2WeylElement_mem_normalizer_diagonalTorus); the Borel subgroup with its order (GL2Borel.card_eq); conjugacy of non-scalar elements by trace and determinant (isConj_iff_of_notMem_range_scalar, conjClassesGLFinTwoEquiv). The node adds: the basis-free definitions (a pair of lines; a quadratic subfield of End_k(V)) and their identification with these models up to conjugacy; the normalisers, with [N(C) : C] = 2 and trace 0, scalar square off C; the images in PGL(V); half-Cartans; Serre's Proposition 14.
acceptance: |C_s| = (q − 1)², |C_ns| = q² − 1, |N(C_s)| = 2(q − 1)², |N(C_ns)| = 2(q² − 1); for q = 3, N(C_s) is dihedral of order 8 and N(C_ns) is the semidihedral Sylow 2-subgroup of GL_2(F_3) of order 16.

nodes.title: p-subgroups of GL_2 in characteristic p fix a unique line
nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic p > 0 (finite or algebraically closed) and P ⊂ GL_2(k) a nontrivial finite p-subgroup. Then every element of P is unipotent, P is elementary abelian of exponent p, conjugate into the upper unitriangular group {[[1, b], [0, 1]]} ≅ (k, +), and P fixes exactly one line D = V^P of k̄² (which is k-rational); the normaliser of P in GL_2(k) lies in the Borel subgroup B(D). Consequently: (i) a subgroup G ⊂ GL_2(k) with a nontrivial normal p-subgroup is reducible, with G-stable line V^{O_p(G)}; (ii) the Sylow p-subgroups of GL_2(F_q) are the unipotent radicals of the q + 1 Borel subgroups, of order q; (iii) for G ⊂ GL_2(k) reducible over k̄ with p | |G|, the Sylow p-subgroup of G is normal and fixes the unique G-stable line; (iv) a finite subgroup of PGL_2(k̄) with a nontrivial normal p-subgroup fixes a point of P¹(k̄).
hypotheses: char k = p > 0
P finite (for k finite automatic)
proofSteps: An element u of p-power order satisfies (u − 1)^{p^a} = u^{p^a} − 1 = 0, so u is unipotent; in dimension 2, (u − 1)² = 0, hence u^p = 1.

For u ≠ 1 unipotent, ker(u − 1) is the unique u-invariant line. By step [0] every element of P is unipotent, so tauceti:Representation.exists_basis_isUpperUnitriangular_of_isUnipotent (a finite-dimensional representation of a monoid by unipotent operators over a field is upper unitriangular in some basis) gives a basis of k² in which P is upper unitriangular: a conjugate of P lies in the Borel subgroup (lower-left entry 0, tauceti:TauCeti.GL2Borel.mem_iff) with diagonal entries 1, so P is isomorphic to a subgroup of (k, +), and the first basis vector spans a line fixed pointwise by P. All non-identity elements of P then share that line. The library statement gives existence of the line; the node adds its uniqueness, its rationality, the normaliser and (i)–(iv).

If g normalises P then g permutes the P-fixed lines, of which there is one; so g ∈ B(D). (i) follows since O_p(G) is characteristic in G (Mathlib IsPGroup, Sylow). For (iv), let H̃ ⊂ SL_2(k̄) be the preimage of H ⊂ PGL_2(k̄) = SL_2(k̄)/{±1}, a finite group, and Ñ the preimage of the normal p-subgroup. Ñ is a central extension of a p-group by {±1}, so it has a unique Sylow p-subgroup P (P = Ñ if p = 2, where −1 = 1; Ñ = {±1} × P if p is odd); P is characteristic in Ñ, hence normal in H̃, and P ≠ 1, so (i) gives an H̃-stable line, a fixed point of H.

(ii) |GL_2(F_q)| = (q − 1)²·q(q + 1) is tauceti:TauCeti.natCard_GL_fin_two. The Borel subgroup B, the stabiliser of ∞ in the Möbius action on the projective line (tauceti:TauCeti.GL2Borel.stabilizer_infty), has order q(q − 1)² (tauceti:TauCeti.GL2Borel.card_eq) and index q + 1 (tauceti:TauCeti.GL2Borel.index_eq), so it has q + 1 conjugates, the stabilisers of the q + 1 points. In the coordinates tauceti:TauCeti.GL2Borel.equivProd (B ≃ (F_q^× × F_q^×) × F_q) the unipotent radical is the fibre over (1, 1), of order q, the full power of p in |GL_2(F_q)|; so the unipotent radicals of the Borel subgroups are the Sylow p-subgroups (mathlib:Sylow).
acceptance: For q = 4: the Sylow 2-subgroups of SL_2(F_4) ≅ A_5 are the five Klein four-groups, the unipotent radicals of the five Borels; this is the exclusion of A_4 in characteristic 2.
Over F_3 the group SL_2(F_3) has Sylow 3-subgroups of order 3 that are not normal (four of them), so SL_2(F_3) is irreducible; consistent with (iii).

For a finite Galois extension E/ℚ_p with wild inertia P ≠ 1 embedded in GL_2(F) (char F = p), the image of the decomposition group lies in a Borel and P maps into its unipotent radical (SmallRamificationAndAbelianVarietyBaseCases:R25.1/wild-image-borel-normal-form).

nodes.title: Dickson: subgroups of PSL_2(F_s) with more than one Sylow p-subgroup
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime, s = p^n, and H a subgroup of PSL_2(F_s) (the image of SL_2(F_s) in PGL_2(F_s)) whose order is divisible by p. For μ ∈ P¹(F_s) let U_μ ⊂ PSL_2(F_s) be the group, of order s, of unipotent elements fixing μ. Every element of order p of H lies in exactly one U_μ; the non-trivial groups H ∩ U_μ are the Sylow p-subgroups of H, of a common order p^m, and their number is 1 + f·p^m for an integer f ≥ 0. (i) If f = 0, H fixes a point of P¹(F_s). (ii) If f ≥ 1, then m divides n and, after conjugation of H by an element of PGL_2(F_s), exactly one of the following holds: (A) p^m > 2, f = 1 and H = PSL_2(F_{p^m}); (A₂) p^m = 2 and H is dihedral of order 2(1 + 2f) (for f = 1 it is PSL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3); (B) p is odd, n/m is even, f = 1 and H = PGL_2(F_{p^m}); (B₃) p = 3, m = 1, n is even, f = 3, and H has order 60 and is isomorphic to A_5.
hypotheses: s = p^n; H is any subgroup of PSL_2(F_s) of order divisible by p
the conjugation in (ii) is by an element of PGL_2(F_s), which may lie outside PSL_2(F_s)
Dickson's notation: G_{M(s)} = PSL_2(F_s) of order M(s) = s(s² − 1)/(2;1), G_{2M(p^k)} = PGL_2(F_{p^k}), G_Ω = H, (2;1) = 2 for p odd and 1 for p = 2
the proof is Dickson's counting argument, Dickson 1901 §§251–254, printed pp. 272–279
proofSteps: Dickson §251 (printed pp. 272–273). An element of order p of PSL_2(F_s) fixes exactly one point of the projective line (R01.4/p-subgroups-and-borel-subgroups), so the elements of order p of H are distributed over the groups H ∩ U_μ. Let H ∩ U_∞ have maximal order p^m > 1. Conjugation by H ∩ U_∞ permutes the other non-trivial H ∩ U_μ in orbits of length p^m, so H ∩ U_∞ is one of 1 + f·p^m conjugates under H, and a counting of class sizes shows that every non-trivial H ∩ U_μ is one of them. They are the Sylow p-subgroups of H (mathlib:Sylow). If f = 0, H ∩ U_∞ is normal in H and H fixes ∞ (R01.4/p-subgroups-and-borel-subgroups (iv)): this is (i), treated in Dickson §§249–250.

Dickson §251 (p. 273). The stabiliser of ∞ in H is (H ∩ U_∞) ⋊ C_d with C_d cyclic of order d, generated by a diagonal substitution z ↦ η²z, so |H| = (1 + f p^m)·p^m·d. After conjugation by a diagonal element of PGL_2(F_s), the additive group Λ = {λ : z ↦ z + λ ∈ H} contains 1; Λ is a vector space over its multiplier field GF[p^k] = {κ : κΛ ⊂ Λ}, k | m, and each η² is a multiplier.

Dickson §251 (pp. 273–274). H is the union of the stabiliser of ∞ and f·p^m cosets of it, with representatives V_j = (α_j, β_j; γ_j, δ_j), γ_j ≠ 0. There are f p^m (p^m − 1) elements of order p outside U_∞; an element V_{η,λ}V_j has order p iff α_jη + δ_jη⁻¹ + γ_jηλ = ±2 (Dickson's relation 251)), which for given V_j and η has at most (2;1) solutions λ. Comparing the two counts gives his inequality 252): p^m − 1 ≤ (2;1)d ≤ (2,1;1)(p^k − 1) ≤ (2,1;1)(p^m − 1), hence p^m < 2p^k, m = k and Λ = GF[p^k]. Two cases remain: [A] (2;1)d = p^k − 1; [B] p > 2, n/k even, d = p^k − 1.

Dickson §252 (pp. 274–276), case [A]. For p^k > 2 relation 253) (and separate arguments for p^k = 3 and for p = 2, k > 1) puts the coefficients of every V_j in GF[p^k], so H ⊂ PSL_2(F_{p^k}); comparing orders, f = 1 and H = PSL_2(F_{p^k}): (A). For p^k = 2 the 1 + 2f involutions of H are conjugate, the products of a fixed one with the others form a cyclic group of order 1 + 2f which it inverts, and H is dihedral of order 2(1 + 2f): (A₂).

Dickson §253 (pp. 276–278), case [B]. Counting the elements of order 2 of the form V_{η,λ}V_j in two ways gives inequality 255): ½(f p^k − 1)p^k ≤ p^k(p^k − 1) + (f − 1)p^k, that is, f·(p^k − 2) ≤ 2p^k − 3. Dickson shows first that ½(1 + f p^k) is an integer, so that f is odd (p. 277); with f odd the inequality gives f = 1, or f = 3 with p^k = 3. For f = 1 the coset representatives can be chosen with coefficients in GF[p^k] up to the factor √κ_0 (κ_0 a primitive root of GF[p^k]) and H = PGL_2(F_{p^k}): (B). For f = 3 and p^k = 3, |H| = 60, H has ten Sylow 3-subgroups and fifteen involutions lying in five conjugate four-groups; by §254 (pp. 278–279) H acts faithfully on the five four-groups and is the alternating group on five letters (mathlib:alternatingGroup): (B₃).
acceptance: In PSL_2(F_9) ≅ A_6 (p = 3, n = 2) the subgroups with more than one Sylow 3-subgroup are, up to conjugacy in PGL_2(F_9): A_4 = PSL_2(F_3) (case (A), four Sylow subgroups, f = 1), S_4 = PGL_2(F_3) (case (B)), A_5 (case (B₃), ten Sylow subgroups, f = 3), and A_6 itself (case (A) with m = 2, ten Sylow subgroups of order 9).

In PSL_2(F_4) ≅ A_5 (p = 2): the dihedral groups of order 6 and 10 (case (A₂), f = 1, 2) and A_5 itself (case (A), m = 2, five Sylow 2-subgroups); A_4 has a normal Sylow 2-subgroup and fixes a point (f = 0).

In SL_2(F_9), [[1, 1], [0, 1]] and [[1, 0], [λ, 1]] with λ² = −1 generate a group of order 120 whose image in PSL_2(F_9) is the A_5 of case (B₃); for the other four λ generating F_9 they generate SL_2(F_9). In SL_2(F_4) two involutions with distinct fixed points generate a dihedral group of order 6 or 10, and in SL_2(F_8) one of order 6, 14 or 18 (case (A₂) with f = 1, 2, resp. f = 1, 3, 4): [[1, 1], [0, 1]] and [[1, 0], [b, 1]] generate a group of order 6 exactly when b = 1, of order 10 for the two other b ≠ 0 of F_4, and of order 14 or 18 (three values of b each) for the six other b ≠ 0 of F_8.

nodes.title: Finite subgroups of PGL_2 of order prime to the characteristic: cyclic, dihedral, A_4, S_4, A_5
nodes.statement: Let K be an algebraically closed field and H ⊂ PGL_2(K) a finite subgroup whose order Ω is not divisible by the characteristic of K (no condition in characteristic 0). Then H is cyclic, or dihedral of order 2n with n ≥ 2, or Ω ∈ {12, 24, 60} and H is isomorphic to A_4, S_4, A_5 respectively. More precisely, every non-identity element of H lies in exactly one maximal cyclic subgroup of H; if d_1, …, d_r are the orders of representatives of the conjugacy classes of maximal cyclic subgroups and f_i ∈ {1, 2} the index of each in its normaliser in H, then 1 − Σ_i (d_i − 1)/(f_i d_i) = 1/Ω, r ≤ 3, and the solutions are: r = 1 (cyclic); r = 2 with (d_1, d_2) = (2, n), n odd (dihedral) or (3, 2), Ω = 12 (A_4); r = 3 with (n, 2, 2), n even (dihedral), (4, 3, 2), Ω = 24 (S_4), (5, 3, 2), Ω = 60 (A_5). Consequently every element of A_4, S_4, A_5 ⊂ PGL_2(K) has order 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5, and the statement holds for finite subgroups of PGL_2(k) for any field k of characteristic not dividing Ω (Serre 1972, Proposition 16).
hypotheses: K algebraically closed; H finite with char K ∤ |H| (automatic in characteristic 0)

Dickson states and proves this for subgroups of PSL_2(F_s) containing no operators of period p; the count uses only that non-identity elements are diagonalisable, so it is the same over any algebraically closed field
for a field k that is not algebraically closed apply the statement to PGL_2(k) ⊂ PGL_2(k̄)
proofSteps: An element of H of order d > 1 lifts to a matrix of finite order prime to char K, hence diagonalisable and non-scalar; it has exactly two fixed points on P¹(K) and lies in a unique maximal torus T of PGL_2(K), the stabiliser of the two points, T ≅ K^× (for K = F̄_p this is the Cartan subgroup containing it, R01.4/cartan-subgroups-and-normalisers). H ∩ T is a finite subgroup of K^×, hence cyclic (mathlib:isCyclic_subgroup_units); these groups H ∩ T ≠ 1 are the maximal cyclic subgroups of H, and two distinct ones meet in the identity (Dickson §256, quoting his §§242–243).

The normaliser of T in PGL_2(K) is T ⋊ ℤ/2 (the elements preserving the pair of fixed points), and an element of H normalising C = H ∩ T ≠ 1 normalises T. So N_H(C) is C, or contains C with index 2 and is then dihedral (elements outside T invert T). Hence C has Ω/(f·d) conjugates in H with d = |C| and f ∈ {1, 2}.

Counting the non-identity elements of H by maximal cyclic subgroups gives Dickson's relation 256): Ω = 1 + Σ_i (d_i − 1)·Ω/(f_i d_i), i.e. 259): 1 − Σ_i (d_i − 1)/(f_i d_i) = 1/Ω. Each term is ≥ 1/4, so r ≤ 3 (Dickson, p. 281).

Case analysis (Dickson, pp. 281–282). r = 1: f_1 = 1 and Ω = d_1, H cyclic. r = 2: (f_1, f_2) = (1, 2) up to order, d_1 < 4; d_1 = 2 gives Ω = 2d_2 and H dihedral with d_2 odd; d_1 = 3 gives d_2 = 2, Ω = 12, with four conjugate subgroups of order 3 and three involutions forming a normal four-group, so H ≅ A_4 (mathlib:alternatingGroup). r = 3: all f_i = 2 and 1 + 2/Ω = 1/d_1 + 1/d_2 + 1/d_3; one d_i is 2; if two are, H is dihedral of order 2d_1 with d_1 even (mathlib:DihedralGroup); otherwise (d_1, 3, 2) with d_1 ∈ {3, 4, 5} and Ω = 12, 24, 60, and d_1 = 3 is excluded by relation 258) (two non-conjugate cyclic subgroups of odd orders d_i, d_j force Ω ≥ d_i(d_j − 1) + d_j(d_i − 1) + 1).

Identification. Ω = 24, (4, 3, 2): H has four subgroups of order 3 and acts on them by conjugation; the kernel lies in a normaliser of order 6 and is trivial (it cannot contain a subgroup of order 3, which is not normal, and a normal subgroup of order 2 would be central, whereas the centraliser of an element of order 3 is contained in its torus), so H ≅ S_4 (mathlib:Equiv.Perm; Dickson §248). Ω = 60, (5, 3, 2): H has ten subgroups of order 3 and fifteen involutions in five conjugate four-groups, acts faithfully on these five four-groups, and is the alternating group on five letters (Dickson §254, pp. 278–279).
acceptance: PGL_2(F_7), of order 336 = 2⁴·3·7: its subgroups of order prime to 7 are cyclic, dihedral, A_4 (14 of them) or S_4 (14 of them), none is A_5; found by listing all 413 subgroups.
For K = ℂ this is the classification of the finite subgroups of PGL_2(ℂ) (Darmon–Diamond–Taylor Theorem 2.47(a)): C_n, D_{2n}, A_4, S_4, A_5.
