nodes.title: m-th roots of ℓ-adic characters up to characters of finite order
nodes.statement: Let Γ be a profinite group, ℓ a prime, χ : Γ → Q̄_ℓ^× a continuous character and m a non-zero integer. Then there are continuous characters χ_1, χ_0 : Γ → Q̄_ℓ^× with χ_0 of finite order and χ = χ_1^m·χ_0. (Patrikis, Lemma 2.3.15, is the case Γ = G_F for a number field F.) The factor χ_0 cannot be dropped in general.
hypotheses: continuity for the ℓ-adic topology of Q̄_ℓ; values in Q̄_ℓ^× and not in a fixed finite extension: the root χ_1 may need a larger coefficient field
no hypothesis on Γ beyond profinite (compactness is what is used)
proofSteps: Coefficients: χ(Γ) is compact, so it lies in O_E^× for a finite extension E/Q_ℓ (R01.1/baire-descent-to-a-finite-coefficient-field).

Structure of O_E^×: it is μ′ × (1 + 𝔪_E) with μ′ finite of order prime to ℓ, and 1 + 𝔪_E is a finitely generated Z_ℓ-module (z·u = u^z). Hence the closed subgroup C = χ(Γ) is F × L with F finite and L a free Z_ℓ-module of finite rank s (structure of finitely generated modules over the principal ideal domain Z_ℓ, and a choice of complement to the torsion). Let χ_0 be χ followed by the projection to F and χ_L the projection to L; both are continuous characters, χ = χ_0χ_L and χ_0 has finite order.

Roots on L: write m = ℓ^a m′ with ℓ ∤ m′. Choose a Z_ℓ-basis x_1,…,x_s of L and y_i ∈ Q̄_ℓ with y_i^{ℓ^a} = x_i; since x_i ≡ 1 modulo the maximal ideal and ℓ-power roots of unity are trivial in characteristic ℓ, y_i ∈ 1 + 𝔪_{E′} for E′ = E(y_1,…,y_s). The map ψ : L → 1 + 𝔪_{E′}, ∏ x_i^{z_i} ↦ ∏ y_i^{z_i}, is a continuous homomorphism with ψ^{ℓ^a} the inclusion. Put χ_1 = (ψ ∘ χ_L)^{1/m′}, where 1/m′ ∈ Z_ℓ acts on the Z_ℓ-module 1 + 𝔪_{E′}. Then χ_1^m = χ_L.
acceptance: ℓ odd, Γ = G_Q, χ = χ_ℓ the cyclotomic character, m = 2: χ_ℓ = ⟨χ_ℓ⟩·ω with ⟨χ_ℓ⟩ valued in 1 + ℓZ_ℓ and ω the Teichmüller character; χ_1 = ⟨χ_ℓ⟩^{1/2} and χ_0 = ω, of order ℓ − 1.
χ of finite order: χ_1 = 1 and χ_0 = χ.
χ_0 is needed: χ_ℓ(c) = −1 for a complex conjugation c ∈ G_Q, and χ_1(c)^2 = χ_1(c^2) = 1 for every character χ_1, so χ_ℓ is not a square of a character of G_Q.

sources.match: Patrikis's Lemma 2.3.15 (stated for Γ_F, with reference to [Con11, Lemma 3.1]): χ = (χ_1)^m χ_0 with χ_0 of finite order. The lemma here is the same statement for any profinite group, with a proof.

nodes.title: Lifts of geometric projective representations: half-integral Hodge–Tate–Sen weights, and Hodge–Tate lifts over totally real fields
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field and ℓ a prime. Hodge–Tate weights are labelled and normalised as in PadicHodgeTheory:R06.2/hodge-tate-weight-convention (HT(χ_ℓ) = +1), and Hodge–Tate–Sen weights are the eigenvalues of Sen's operator (PadicHodgeTheory:P7/sen-module). (1) (Patrikis, Lemma 2.7.4) Let P : G_F → PGL_2(Q̄_ℓ) be continuous and geometric: unramified at all but finitely many places, and ad⁰ of one (equivalently every) lift is de Rham at the places above ℓ. Then P has a lift ρ : G_F → GL_2(Q̄_ℓ) (G7/lifting-projective-representations) whose Hodge–Tate–Sen weights at all v | ℓ lie in (1/2)Z; one can take det ρ of finite order. For every lift ρ with weights in (1/2)Z, Sym^2 ρ and det ρ are geometric. (2) (BCGP21, proof of Proposition 9.2.1) Let F be totally real, F′/F a quadratic extension (not assumed totally real: BCGP21 assume nothing on F′) and s : G_{F′} → GL_2(Q̄_ℓ) continuous, unramified at all but finitely many places and de Rham at the places above ℓ with Hodge–Tate weights {−1, 0} for every embedding (BCGP21 write (0, 1), in their convention HT(ε) = {−1}), such that Proj s extends to a continuous P : G_F → PGL_2(Q̄_ℓ). Then P lifts to a continuous r̃ : G_F → GL_2(Q̄_ℓ) that is unramified almost everywhere and Hodge–Tate with weights {−1, 0} at every v | ℓ and every embedding, and r̃|_{G_{F′}} = s ⊗ ψ for a character ψ of G_{F′} of finite order.
hypotheses: F a number field; in (2) F is totally real (Patrikis Lemma 2.3.17 is applied to the character det r̃ of G_F) and F′ is an arbitrary quadratic extension of F
geometric is a condition on the projective representation: it is tested on ad⁰ of a lift, which does not depend on the lift
the lift in (1) is in general not Hodge–Tate: for the projectivised Tate module of an elliptic curve over a totally real field no lift with determinant of finite order is, since its weights are ±1/2
proofSteps: (1), existence: take a lift ρ_0 of P, unramified almost everywhere (G7/lifting-projective-representations). By G7/roots-of-characters-up-to-finite-order with m = 2, det ρ_0 = ψ^2χ_0 with χ_0 of finite order; put ρ = ρ_0 ⊗ ψ^{−1}, so det ρ = χ_0. In rank two and characteristic 0, Sym^2 ρ ≅ ad⁰ ρ ⊗ det ρ (G7/adjoint-representations) and ρ ⊗ ρ ≅ Sym^2 ρ ⊕ det ρ (G7/symmetric-and-exterior-powers), so ρ ⊗ ρ is de Rham, in particular Hodge–Tate, at each v | ℓ. Sen's operator of ρ ⊗ ρ is Θ ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ Θ (requested from PadicHodgeTheory), so for the eigenvalues a, b of Θ_ρ at an embedding, 2a, a + b and 2b are integers: a, b ∈ (1/2)Z. This route does not use the theorem of Wintenberger and Conrad (Patrikis, Theorem 2.1.6), to which Patrikis appeals.

(1), every lift with weights in (1/2)Z: ad⁰ ρ is Hodge–Tate, so a − b ∈ Z and then a + b = (a − b) + 2b ∈ Z. The character det ρ has integral Hodge–Tate–Sen weight, so it is Hodge–Tate, hence de Rham (PadicHodgeTheory:R06.2/hodge-tate-characters-are-de-rham), and Sym^2 ρ ≅ ad⁰ ρ ⊗ det ρ is de Rham. Both are unramified almost everywhere because ρ is (G7/lifting-projective-representations (3)).

(2): P is geometric, because ad⁰ of a lift of P restricts on G_{F′} to ad⁰ s and being de Rham or unramified can be tested on an open subgroup. Take r̃ as in (1); r̃|_{G_{F′}} and s have the same projectivisation, so r̃|_{G_{F′}} = s ⊗ ψ for a continuous character ψ of G_{F′}, whose Hodge–Tate–Sen weights lie in (1/2)Z. For an embedding τ′ of F′ above an embedding τ of F, the weights of r̃ at τ are those of s ⊗ ψ at τ′, namely {x_{τ′} − 1, x_{τ′}} with x_{τ′} the weight of ψ at τ′; so x_{τ′} = x_τ depends only on τ, and the character det r̃ of G_F has weight 2x_τ − 1 at τ. By Patrikis Lemma 2.3.17 (F totally real) these weights are all equal, so x_τ = x ∈ (1/2)Z for every τ. There is a character θ of G_F with all Hodge–Tate–Sen weights −x (G7/roots-of-characters-up-to-finite-order with m = 2 applied to χ_ℓ^{−2x}); replace r̃ by r̃ ⊗ θ. Now ψ has all weights 0, so r̃|_{G_{F′}} is Hodge–Tate with the weights of s, and so is r̃ (finite extension). A character with Sen operator 0 has finite image on inertia at the places above ℓ (PadicHodgeTheory:R06.2/hodge-tate-characters-are-de-rham) and ψ is unramified almost everywhere, so ψ has finite order by class field theory (BCGP21 p. 254: 'Since ψ is Hodge–Tate of weight 0, it has finite order').
acceptance: BCGP21, Proposition 9.2.1, type E[D_n]: s = s_l is a member of a weakly compatible system with s^σ ≅ s ⊗ δ; Proj s extends to G_F by Schur's lemma and (2) gives r̃ with r̃|_{G_{F′}} = s ⊗ ψ.

For E an elliptic curve over a totally real F and P the projectivisation of V_ℓE: the lift V_ℓE has weights {0, 1}; a lift with determinant of finite order is V_ℓE ⊗ ψ^{−1} with ψ^2 = χ_ℓ·(finite order), of Hodge–Tate–Sen weights {−1/2, 1/2}: in (1/2)Z and not Hodge–Tate, and Sym^2 of it is ad⁰(V_ℓE) twisted by a character of finite order.

nodes.title: From determinants to representations, only through IHG.1, and compatibility with the operations
nodes.statement: Let Γ be profinite and D an n-dimensional continuous determinant on A[Γ] (IntegralHeckeAndGaloisDeterminants:IHG.0/continuous-determinant). G7 produces a representation from D only in the two situations supplied by IHG.1, with its hypotheses: (a) A = k one of the algebraically closed coefficient fields of R01.1 (F̄_p with the discrete topology, Q̄_ℓ with its ℓ-adic topology): there is a continuous semisimple ρ : Γ → GL_n(k), unique up to isomorphism, with det ∘ ρ = D (Chenevier Theorem 2.12 with continuity); (b) A complete local Noetherian with finite residue field and D̄ := D ⊗ k absolutely irreducible: there is a continuous ρ : Γ → GL_n(A), unique up to GL_n(A)-conjugacy, with det ∘ ρ = D (Chenevier Theorem 2.22). In both cases ρ is an object of ContinuousRep Γ A (R01.1) and the operations of G7 are compatible with determinants: for Φ ∈ {Sym^k, ∧^k, T^k, dual, twist by a character, ad, ad⁰ and ad/A·1 (for every n: det(X − ad ρ(g)) = (X − 1)·det(X − g | ad⁰ ρ) = (X − 1)·det(X − g | ad ρ/A·1)), ⊗ with another such representation, restriction to open subgroups, coefficient extension} the determinant det ∘ Φ(ρ) depends only on D (and the other inputs' determinants), via the characteristic-polynomial identities of G7/symmetric-and-exterior-powers. Polarizations transfer in case (b) when 2 ∈ A^×: if D^c = D^∨·μ|_{G_F} (equality of determinants on G_F) then ρ admits a polarization with multiplier μ or μδ_{F/F⁺}, and its pairing is unique up to A^× (over the residue field this is CHT Lemma 2.1.4). When 2 ∉ A^× a covariant perfect pairing still exists and is unique up to A^×, with ⟨y, x⟩ = ε⟨x, y⟩ for some ε ∈ μ_2(A); it makes a CHT triple (G7/polarized-representation (c)) with multiplier μη, η the character of Gal(F/F⁺) with η(c_v) = −εμ(c_v)^{−1} ∈ μ_2(A), and μ_2(A) can be larger than {±1}: for A = F_2[t]/(t^2), n = 1, ρ trivial and μ the character of Gal(F/F⁺) with μ(c_v) = 1 + t, no polarization has multiplier μ or μδ_{F/F⁺}. No representation is inferred from a determinant that is residually reducible: there D need not be det ∘ ρ for any ρ over A.
hypotheses: IHG.1 hypotheses are kept exactly: for (a) an algebraically closed field, here F̄_p discrete or Q̄_ℓ (Chenevier's Theorem 2.12 has no topology; the continuity of ρ is part of what is requested from IHG.1); for (b) a complete local Noetherian A with finite residue field and residually absolutely irreducible D̄
the polarization statement in (b) needs D̄ absolutely irreducible, so that the pairing is unique up to scalars (G7/schur-lemma-over-local-rings), and 2 ∈ A^× for the multiplier to be μ or μδ_{F/F⁺}
proofSteps: Existence and uniqueness: IHG.1 (requested; Chenevier Theorems 2.12 and 2.22).

Compatibility: for ρ with det ∘ ρ = D, the characteristic polynomial of Φ(ρ)(g) is a universal polynomial in that of ρ(g) (G7/charpoly-of-symmetric-and-exterior-powers for Sym^k and ∧^k; G7/charpoly-of-cyclically-permuted-tensor-product (4) for tensor products, hence for T^k, twists and ad = ρ ⊗ ρ^∨, the characteristic polynomial of ρ^∨(g) being the reciprocal polynomial of that of ρ(g) divided by det ρ(g); G7/adjoint-representations for ad⁰ and ad/A·1), and the characteristic polynomials of ρ(g) are the coefficients of D (IHG.0); by Amitsur's formula (IntegralHeckeAndGaloisDeterminants:IHG.0/amitsur-formula) the determinant of Φ(ρ) is determined by these.

Polarization: D^c = D^∨μ gives ρ^c ≅ ρ^∨ ⊗ μ over A by the uniqueness in (b), i.e. a matrix P ∈ GL_n(A) with ρ(c_vσc_v)Pᵗρ(σ) = μ(σ)P, unique up to A^× by G7/schur-lemma-over-local-rings (3). The pairing ⟨x, y⟩ = ᵗxP^{−1}y satisfies the covariance identity, and so does (x, y) ↦ ⟨y, x⟩ because c_v^2 = 1; hence ⟨y, x⟩ = ε⟨x, y⟩ with ε ∈ A^×, ε^2 = 1. If 2 ∈ A^× then ε = ±1 and μ(c_v) = ±1 (A is local), and (ρ, μ′) is polarized for the μ′ ∈ {μ, μδ_{F/F⁺}} with μ′(c_v) = −ε. Over the residue field this is G7/polarization-sign-and-determinant (4).
acceptance: Residually reducible non-example: a non-split extension 0 → χ → ρ_1 → 1 → 0 and ρ_2 = 1 ⊕ χ have the same determinant D, so D does not determine a representation up to isomorphism when D̄ is reducible; G7 constructs nothing from such D.
For ρ = ρ_D in case (b), det(Sym^2 ρ) = (det ρ)^3 for n = 2, computed from D alone.

nodes.title: Schur's lemma for residually absolutely irreducible representations over a local ring
nodes.statement: Let A be a commutative local ring with maximal ideal 𝔪 and residue field k, Γ a group and ρ : Γ → GL_n(A) a homomorphism whose reduction ρ̄ : Γ → GL_n(k) is absolutely irreducible. Then (1) the A-submodule of M_n(A) spanned by ρ(Γ) is M_n(A); (2) every X ∈ M_n(A) commuting with ρ(Γ) is a scalar matrix: End_{A[Γ]}(A^n) = A, and the centraliser of ρ(Γ) in GL_n(A) is A^×; (3) if ρ′ : Γ → GL_n(A) is a second homomorphism and P, P′ ∈ GL_n(A) satisfy ρ′(g)P = Pρ(g) and ρ′(g)P′ = P′ρ(g) for all g, then P′ = aP with a ∈ A^×. No completeness, Noetherian or topological hypothesis is used. (CHT08, Lemma 2.1.8, is (2) for Noetherian complete local rings and continuous ρ.)
hypotheses: A local; ρ̄ absolutely irreducible (irreducible is not enough: over ℝ the rotation representation of ℤ/4 on ℝ^2 has commutant ℂ)
proofSteps: (1): by Burnside's theorem (R01.1/absolutely-irreducible, condition (iii)) the k-span of ρ̄(Γ) is M_n(k). Let S ⊂ M_n(A) be the A-span of ρ(Γ). Then M_n(A) = S + 𝔪·M_n(A), and M_n(A) is a finitely generated A-module, so S = M_n(A) by Nakayama's lemma (Mathlib Submodule.le_of_le_smul_of_le_jacobson_bot, with 𝔪 the Jacobson radical of the local ring A).
(2): X commutes with S = M_n(A), so X lies in the centre of M_n(A), which consists of the scalar matrices (Mathlib Matrix.center_eq_range); a scalar matrix in GL_n(A) has its scalar in A^×.
(3): P^{−1}P′ commutes with ρ(Γ), hence is a scalar a, and a ∈ A^× because P^{−1}P′ is invertible.
acceptance: A = k a field: Schur's lemma for an absolutely irreducible representation, End_Γ(V) = k.

A = ℤ/4, Γ = S_3, ρ generated by (0 1; 1 0) and (0 −1; 1 −1): the reduction modulo 2 is the irreducible two-dimensional representation of S_3 ≅ GL_2(F_2), absolutely irreducible, so every matrix in M_2(ℤ/4) commuting with ρ(S_3) is a scalar.
Without absolute irreducibility: for the trivial representation of rank 2 the centraliser is GL_2(A).

sources.match: CHT08 Lemma 2.1.8: for a Noetherian complete local ring R and ρ continuous with ρ mod m_R absolutely irreducible, the centraliser of the image is R^×. The lemma here drops the Noetherian, completeness and continuity hypotheses (Burnside and Nakayama) and includes non-invertible endomorphisms.

nodes.title: Adequate, weakly adequate and GHT-adequate subgroups of GL_n over a field of characteristic p
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime, k a field of characteristic p, n ≥ 1, V = k^n and H ⊆ GL_n(k) a finite subgroup. Let ad = M_n(k) = End_k(V) with H acting by conjugation h·X = hXh⁻¹ (the representation G7/adjoint-representations, i.e. Mathlib's linHom of the tautological representation with itself), ad⁰ ⊆ ad the H-submodule of trace-zero matrices, and ad₀ := ad/k·1 the quotient by the scalar line; ad⁰ → ad → ad₀ is an isomorphism exactly when p ∤ n, and the three modules are kept distinct. An element g ∈ H is semisimple if it is diagonalisable over an algebraic closure k̄; as H is finite this holds exactly when the order of g is prime to p. For g ∈ H and α ∈ k̄ write e_{g,α} ∈ M_n(k̄) for the g-equivariant projection of k̄^n onto the generalised α-eigenspace of g along the sum of the other generalised eigenspaces. (a) H is weakly adequate if the semisimple elements of H span M_n(k) as a k-vector space. (b) H is adequate (Thorne 2012, Definition 2.3; equivalently BLGG13, Definition A.1.1) if (A1) H¹(H, k) = 0, i.e. H has no quotient of order p; (A2) H⁰(H, ad⁰) = 0 and H¹(H, ad⁰) = 0; (A3) for every simple k̄[H]-submodule W ⊆ ad⁰ ⊗_k k̄ there are g ∈ H and an eigenvalue α ∈ k̄ of g with tr(e_{g,α}·W) ≠ 0. (c) H is GHT-adequate (Thorne 2017, Definition 2.20, taken from Guralnick–Herzig–Tiep) if H¹(H, k) = 0, H¹(H, ad₀) = 0, and for every simple k̄[H]-submodule W ⊆ ad ⊗_k k̄ there are a semisimple g ∈ H and α ∈ k̄ with tr(e_{g,α}·W) ≠ 0. Group cohomology is Mathlib's groupCohomology of the finite group H with coefficients in the k-linear representation. For a representation r̄ : Γ → GL_n(k) and a subgroup Γ' ⊆ Γ, 'r̄(Γ') is adequate' means that the finite subgroup r̄(Γ') ⊆ GL_n(k) is adequate.
hypotheses: k has characteristic p > 0 and H is finite; for an infinite subgroup none of the three notions is defined here
(A3) quantifies over simple submodules of ad⁰ ⊗ k̄, not of ad⁰ over k; with k containing every eigenvalue of every element of H this is Thorne's condition over k
adequacy is not absolute irreducibility, not bigness (CHT08, which asks for a multiplicity-one eigenvalue) and not enormous image (G7/enormous-image-and-its-coefficient-extension-invariance)
(b) forces p ∤ n: if p | n the scalar matrices lie in ad⁰ and are H-invariant, so (A2) fails; only (c) can hold when p | n
ad⁰ (trace-zero submodule) and ad₀ (quotient by scalars) are different modules when p | n

Thorne 2012, Definition 2.3 has the standing hypotheses that k is finite, that H acts absolutely irreducibly and that k contains all eigenvalues of all elements of H, and quantifies over irreducible k[H]-submodules of ad⁰; BLGG13, Definition A.1.1 is for finite subgroups of GL_n(F̄_l). Absolute irreducibility is not imposed in (b) because (A3) implies it.

(c) is stated with simple k̄[H]-submodules of ad ⊗ k̄ and α ∈ k̄. Thorne 2017, Definition 2.20 is stated over K itself (simple K[H]-submodules of ad and an eigenvalue α ∈ K), and Guralnick–Herzig–Tiep state the third condition as: the semisimple elements span End(V), for V absolutely irreducible. Thorne's form implies the other two (each e_{σ,α} with α ∈ K is a K-polynomial in σ), and the three agree when K contains the eigenvalues of the semisimple elements of H, in particular for K algebraically closed.
proofSteps: Construct ad, ad⁰ and ad₀ from G7/adjoint-representations: ad⁰ is the kernel of Matrix.traceLinearMap (Mathlib LieAlgebra.SpecialLinear.sl as a submodule) and ad₀ is the quotient by the H-stable line k·1; record that ad⁰ ⊆ ad → ad₀ is an isomorphism iff the trace of 1, namely n, is a unit in k. A 'simple k̄[H]-submodule' is a subrepresentation that is irreducible in the sense of Mathlib's Representation.IsIrreducible. H⁰ and H¹ are Mathlib's groupCohomology (groupCohomology.H0, groupCohomology.H1) of the abstract finite group H with coefficients in an object of Rep k H; 'H⁰(H, M) = 0' is read through groupCohomology.H0Iso as the vanishing of Representation.invariants.

Define e_{g,α} as the projection onto Module.End.maxGenEigenspace of g at α along the sum of the other maximal generalised eigenspaces (k̄^n is their direct sum because the characteristic polynomial splits over k̄). 'g semisimple' means that the minimal polynomial of g is separable, i.e. g is diagonalisable over k̄. For g of finite order m this holds iff p ∤ m: if p ∤ m the minimal polynomial divides the separable polynomial X^m − 1; conversely, if g is semisimple of order p·m′ then g^{m′} is semisimple with (g^{m′} − 1)^p = 0, so g^{m′} = 1. For elements of finite order prime to p this agrees with Mathlib's Module.End.IsSemisimple over k (Module.End.isSemisimple_of_squarefree_aeval_eq_zero applied to X^m − 1); over an imperfect field k the two notions differ in general (Module.End.IsSemisimple does not imply diagonalisable over k̄), which is why the definition is stated with the minimal polynomial.

GHTT appendix Lemma 1 (stated for H irreducible; the proof does not use irreducibility): (A3) is equivalent to: the semisimple elements of H span ad. Let U ⊆ ad ⊗ k̄ be the annihilator of the span of the semisimple elements under the trace pairing; U ⊆ ad⁰ ⊗ k̄ (take g = 1) and U is H-stable. For g ∈ H with semisimple part g_s (a power of g, as H is finite), e_{g,α} = e_{g_s,α} is a polynomial in g_s and g_s = Σ_α α·e_{g_s,α}; so a simple submodule W violates (A3) exactly when W ⊆ U, and (A3) holds iff U = 0 iff the semisimple elements span. The same argument for submodules of ad ⊗ k̄ gives the equivalence with the third condition of (c). A subset spanning M_n(k) spans M_n(k̄) and leaves no proper nonzero subspace of k̄^n invariant, so weak adequacy implies absolute irreducibility (the easy converse of Burnside's theorem; Thorne 2017, after Definition 2.20). Hence (A3), and the third condition of (c), imply absolute irreducibility, which Thorne 2012 and Guralnick–Herzig–Tiep impose as a standing hypothesis.
For p ∤ n, ad = k ⊕ ad⁰ as H-modules and ad₀ ≅ ad⁰, so (b) and (c) coincide for absolutely irreducible H (GHT17, introduction: H¹(G,(V*⊗V)/k) is H¹(G, ad⁰) when p ∤ dim V).

Base change: for a field extension k'/k and i = 0, 1, H^i(H, M ⊗_k k') = H^i(H, M) ⊗_k k' for finite H and finite-dimensional M (G7/vanishing-of-h0-and-h1-under-extension-of-the-coefficient-field), and the k-span of a set of matrices has the same dimension after ⊗ k'; so (a), (b), (c) for H ⊆ GL_n(k) are unchanged when k is replaced by k'. BLGG13 Lemma A.1.4 adds invariance under H ↦ k₁^×H for finite k₁ ⊇ k (normal subgroup of index prime to p plus inflation–restriction, Mathlib groupCohomology.H1InfRes_exact).
acceptance: SL₂(F_7) ⊆ GL₂(F_7) is adequate: no quotient of order 7 (perfect, Mathlib Matrix.SL2.commutator_eq_top), H⁰(ad⁰) = 0 and H¹(ad⁰) = 0 (G7/h1-of-sl2-with-adjoint-coefficients (a)), and diag(3, 5), the identity, [[0,1],[−1,0]] and [[0,3],[2,0]] are semisimple and span M₂(F_7).

SL₂(F_5) ⊆ GL₂(F_5) is weakly adequate and absolutely irreducible but not adequate, because H¹(SL₂(F_5), ad⁰) is one-dimensional; SL₂(F_3) ⊆ GL₂(F_3) is not adequate because SL₂(F_3) → A₄ → Z/3 violates (A1), although H⁰ = H¹ = 0 for ad⁰ there (BLGG13 Proposition A.2.1, Points 5 and 6).

GL₂(F_5) ⊆ GL₂(F_5) is adequate: its abelianisation is F_5^× (order 4), and a direct computation gives H¹(GL₂(F_5), ad⁰) = 0 (the class of H¹(SL₂(F_5), ad⁰) is moved by diag(2,1); it survives only in ad⁰ ⊗ det²). This contradicts BLGG13 v1 Proposition A.2.1 for the projective image PGL₂(F_5) (sourceIssues ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations/E754) and agrees with Guralnick–Herzig–Tiep, Corollary 9.5 (projective image PGL₂(p^a) with p^a > 3 and p odd is always adequate) and with Gee–Newton Lemma 3.2.3.
For p | n no subgroup of GL_n(k) is adequate in sense (b); for example SL₂(F_2) ⊆ GL₂(F_2) has H⁰(ad⁰) = k·1 ≠ 0.

nodes.title: Restriction to a subgroup of invertible finite index is injective on H¹ (Mathlib's group cohomology)
nodes.statement: Let k be a commutative ring, G a group, S ≤ G a subgroup of finite index n with n invertible in k, and A a k-linear representation of G (an object of Mathlib's Rep k G; k, G and A in one universe, G an abstract group with no topology). Then a 1-cocycle f : G → A (groupCohomology.IsCocycle₁: f(gh) = g·f(h) + f(g)) whose restriction to S is a coboundary is a coboundary; equivalently the restriction map H¹(G, A) → H¹(S, A) of Mathlib's groupCohomology (groupCohomology.map for the inclusion S → G) is injective. Consequences: (i) if G is finite and #G is invertible in k, then H¹(G, A) = 0; (ii) if G is finite, k is a field of characteristic p and S contains a Sylow p-subgroup of G, then H¹(G, A) → H¹(S, A) is injective, so H¹(G, A) = 0 whenever H¹(S, A) = 0. This is the only form of 'cor ∘ res = index' used by the image conditions of G7; Mathlib has no corestriction for groupCohomology at the pinned commit, and none is constructed here.
hypotheses: the index n = [G : S] must be finite and a unit in k; G itself may be infinite
the statement is for H¹ only; higher degrees are not claimed
proofSteps: From the library: for a transversal t of S in G, Tau Ceti's cochain-level corestriction cor¹_t : (S → A) → (G → A) (TauCeti.ContCohomology.cochainsCor1, defined with no topology for a finite-index subgroup) satisfies cor¹_t(f|_S) = n·f + d⁰(Σ_u f(t u)) for every 1-cocycle f on G (TauCeti.ContCohomology.cochainsCor1_res, stated with Mathlib's groupCohomology.IsCocycle₁) and cor¹_t(d⁰_S a) = d⁰(Σ_u t u·a) (TauCeti.ContCohomology.cochainsCor1_d0). So if f|_S = d⁰_S a, then n·f = d⁰(Σ_u t u·a − Σ_u f(t u)), and f = d⁰(n⁻¹·(…)) is a coboundary (groupCohomology.IsCoboundary₁).

Directly, without the corestriction cochain: subtracting g ↦ g·a − a one may assume f|_S = 0; then f(gs) = g·f(s) + f(g) = f(g), so f is constant on the cosets gS; with b = n⁻¹·Σ_{gS} f(g), h·b = n⁻¹·Σ (f(hg) − f(h)) = b − f(h), so f(h) = h·(−b) − (−b).

Passage to classes: a cocycle has zero class in groupCohomology.H1 iff it is a coboundary (groupCohomology.H1π_eq_zero_iff), and restriction on classes is induced by restriction of cocycles (groupCohomology.map). (i) is the case S = 1: a cocycle on the trivial group is zero. (ii): the index of a subgroup containing a Sylow p-subgroup is prime to p, hence a unit in k.
acceptance: G = Z/2 = ⟨σ⟩ acting on A = F_3 by −1: a cocycle is determined by a = f(σ), and it is the coboundary of x = a (σ·a − a = −2a = a in F_3); H¹ = 0, as (i) says.
Necessity of the hypothesis: G = Z/2 acting trivially on F_2, f(σ) = 1 is a cocycle and not a coboundary, although its restriction to S = 1 is.
SL₂(F_7) ⊇ B (upper triangular, index 8): H¹(SL₂(F_7), M) ↪ H¹(B, M) for every F̄_7[SL₂(F_7)]-module M.

nodes.title: Vanishing of H⁰ and H¹ under extension of the coefficient field
nodes.statement: Let k ⊆ k′ be fields, G a group and M a finite-dimensional k-linear representation of G; put M′ = M ⊗_k k′, a k′-linear representation of G. Cohomology is Mathlib's groupCohomology (groupCohomology.H0, groupCohomology.H1; over k for M, over k′ for M′). (1) (M′)^G = M^G ⊗_k k′; in particular H⁰(G, M) = 0 iff H⁰(G, M′) = 0. (2) A 1-cocycle G → M that becomes a coboundary in M′ is a coboundary in M; so H¹(G, M′) = 0 implies H¹(G, M) = 0. (3) If H⁰(G, M) = 0 and H¹(G, M) = 0, then H¹(G, M′) = 0. (4) If G is finite, H¹(G, M′) ≅ H¹(G, M) ⊗_k k′, so H¹(G, M) = 0 iff H¹(G, M′) = 0. Hence the condition 'H⁰(G, M) = 0 and H¹(G, M) = 0' is invariant under extension of the coefficient field for every group G, and for finite G each of the two vanishing conditions is.
hypotheses: M is finite-dimensional over k; G is arbitrary in (1)–(3) and finite in (4)
for infinite G and infinite k′/k the comparison H¹(G, M′) ≅ H¹(G, M) ⊗ k′ is not claimed: a cocycle into M′ may involve infinitely many elements of a k-basis of k′
proofSteps: (1) is R01.1/coefficient-extension (d).

(2): choose a k-linear retraction π : k′ → k of the inclusion; id ⊗ π : M′ → M is k-linear and G-equivariant and restricts to the identity on M. If f : G → M is a cocycle with f(g) = g·m′ − m′, then f(g) = g·m − m with m = (id ⊗ π)(m′).

(3): let (b_i) be a k-basis of k′ and f : G → M′ a cocycle, f = Σ_i f_i ⊗ b_i with f_i : G → M cocycles (for each g only finitely many f_i(g) are nonzero). By hypothesis f_i(g) = g·m_i − m_i with m_i unique, as M^G = 0. Since M is finite-dimensional there is a finitely generated subgroup G₀ ≤ G with M^{G₀} = M^G = 0; on its finitely many generators only finitely many f_i are nonzero, and for the other i the cocycle f_i vanishes on G₀, so m_i ∈ M^{G₀} = 0. Hence m′ = Σ_i m_i ⊗ b_i is a finite sum and f(g) = g·m′ − m′.

(4): for finite G the cocycles and coboundaries are subspaces of the finite-dimensional space of maps G → M cut out by, respectively spanned by, k-rational linear conditions (groupCohomology.IsCocycle₁, IsCoboundary₁), so both commute with ⊗_k k′.
acceptance: G = Z/3 acting trivially on M = F_3: H¹(G, M) = Hom(Z/3, F_3) is a line over F_3 and H¹(G, M ⊗ F_9) = Hom(Z/3, F_9) is a line over F_9.
(2) for G = Z/2 = ⟨σ⟩ acting on M = F_3 by −1 and k′ = F_9: H¹(G, M ⊗ F_9) = 0 (order prime to 3), hence H¹(G, M) = 0.
(3) is the form needed for an infinite subgroup H ⊆ GL_n(k) with k an infinite algebraic extension of F_p, which the definition of enormous allows: there (4) is not available.

sources.match: The source takes the invariance of conditions (1), (2) of enormity under k′/k for granted; this node proves the cohomological part.

nodes.title: H¹(B, N) embeds into the B-equivariant homomorphisms U → N when the normal subgroup U acts trivially and [B : U] is invertible
nodes.statement: Let k be a commutative ring, B a group, U ⊴ B a normal subgroup of finite index invertible in k, and N a k-linear representation of B on which U acts trivially. For every 1-cocycle f : B → N the restriction f|_U is a homomorphism of groups U → (N, +) with f(b·u·b⁻¹) = b·f(u) for all b ∈ B and u ∈ U; coboundaries restrict to 0; and the resulting map H¹(B, N) → Hom_B(U, N) := {φ ∈ Hom(U, N) : φ(b·u·b⁻¹) = b·φ(u) for all b, u} is injective. In particular H¹(B, N) = 0 if Hom_B(U, N) = 0, and dim_k H¹(B, N) ≤ dim_k Hom_B(U, N) when k is a field. (The map is also surjective; this is not used and not claimed.)
hypotheses: U must act trivially on N; for a general module only G7/h1-restriction-injective-for-invertible-index is available
no action of B/U on H¹(U, N) is used: the equivariance is a property of the restricted cocycle
proofSteps: Additivity: f(uu′) = u·f(u′) + f(u) = f(u′) + f(u), as U acts trivially. Equivariance: f(b·u·b⁻¹) = b·f(u·b⁻¹) + f(b) = b·(u·f(b⁻¹) + f(u)) + f(b) = b·f(u) + (b·f(b⁻¹) + f(b)) = b·f(u) + f(1) = b·f(u), using u·f(b⁻¹) = f(b⁻¹) and f(1) = 0 (both from groupCohomology.IsCocycle₁).
A coboundary b ↦ b·a − a vanishes on U. Under Mathlib's groupCohomology.H1IsoOfIsTrivial for the trivial U-module N, the map is the restriction H¹(B, N) → H¹(U, N) ≅ Hom(U, N).
Injectivity is G7/h1-restriction-injective-for-invertible-index for U ≤ B.
acceptance: B the upper triangular subgroup of SL₂(F_5), U its unipotent subgroup, N = F̄_5 with diag(a, a⁻¹) acting by a^m: as diag(a, a⁻¹)·u(c)·diag(a, a⁻¹)⁻¹ = u(a²c), Hom_B(U, N) = {φ additive : φ(a²c) = a^m·φ(c)} is a line if m ≡ 2 mod 4 and 0 otherwise; so H¹(B, N) = 0 unless m ≡ 2 mod 4.
B = U abelian acting trivially: the map is the identity of Hom(U, N).

sources.match: The source passes from B to its normal subgroup U of index prime to ℓ ('Hⁱ(B, M) ≅ Hⁱ(U, M)^{B/U}'); this node states the part of that isomorphism that Mathlib's carrier gives directly, for modules with trivial U-action.

nodes.title: Vanishing of H¹ of Borel subgroups of GL₂(F_q) with coefficients Sym^k ⊗ det^j, by weights
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime, q = p^r, F = F_q, T′ a subgroup of the diagonal torus of GL₂(F), U = {u(c) = [[1, c], [0, 1]] : c ∈ F} and B = T′U. Let 0 ≤ k ≤ p − 1, j ∈ Z, and M = Sym^k(F̄_p²) ⊗ det^j (the symmetric power of G7/symmetric-and-exterior-powers in the monomial basis) with basis x^{k−i}y^i (0 ≤ i ≤ k), where u(c) fixes x and sends y to y + cx, and t = diag(a, d) multiplies x^{k−i}y^i by χ_i(t) = a^{k−i+j}·d^{i+j}. Call a pair (i, s), 0 ≤ i ≤ k, 0 ≤ s < r, a resonance if χ_i(t) = (a/d)^{p^s} for all t = diag(a, d) ∈ T′. (1) If there is no resonance, H¹(B, M) = 0. (2) If T′ is not contained in the scalars and every resonance has s = 0 and i < k, then H¹(B, M) = 0. (3) In cases (1), (2), H¹(G, M) = 0 for every subgroup G of GL₂(F) containing B with p ∤ [G : B]. Cases: (a) for G = SL₂(F) and its upper triangular subgroup (T′ = {diag(a, a⁻¹)}), j = 0, the resonances are the (i, s) with k − 2i ≡ 2p^s mod (q − 1); if p ≥ 5 and either r ≥ 2 or k ≠ p − 3, every resonance has s = 0 and i < k, so H¹(SL₂(F), Sym^k(F̄_p²)) = 0 for every 0 ≤ k ≤ p − 1 if r ≥ 2, and for every 0 ≤ k ≤ p − 1 with k ≠ p − 3 if r = 1. (b) For G = GL₂(F_p), p ≥ 5, T′ the full diagonal torus, k = 2, j = −1 (M ≅ ad⁰): χ_i = (a/d)^{1−i}, the only resonance is (0, 0), and H¹(GL₂(F_p), ad⁰) = 0, in particular for p = 5. Cohomology is Mathlib's groupCohomology of the finite groups involved.
hypotheses: 0 ≤ k ≤ p − 1 is used twice: the filtration by the monomials is B-stable in any case, but the coefficient i + 1 of the connecting map must be prime to p
a resonance with s ≠ 0 or with i = k is not covered: (a) fails for F = F_p, k = p − 3 (H¹ is one-dimensional) and the lemma says nothing for F_9, k = 2
in (b) the torus is that of GL₂(F_p); for the torus of SL₂(F_5) the pair (2, 0) is a resonance with i = k
proofSteps: Filtration: M_i = ⟨x^{k−l}y^l : l ≤ i⟩ is B-stable and U acts trivially on gr_i = M_i/M_{i−1}, a line on which T′ acts by χ_i, since u(c)·x^{k−i}y^i = x^{k−i}(y + cx)^i ≡ x^{k−i}y^i mod M_{i−1}.

By G7/h1-with-trivial-action-of-a-normal-subgroup (p ∤ [B : U] = #T′), H¹(B, gr_i) ↪ Hom_B(U, gr_i). The additive maps U ≅ F → F̄_p are the Σ_s λ_s·(c ↦ c^{p^s}), 0 ≤ s < r (r linearly independent maps in a space of dimension r), and t·u(c)·t⁻¹ = u((a/d)·c); so Hom_B(U, gr_i) has as basis the maps u(c) ↦ c^{p^s}·x^{k−i}y^i with (i, s) a resonance. With no resonance all H¹(B, gr_i) vanish and (1) follows from the long exact sequences of the filtration (Mathlib groupCohomology.mapShortComplex₂_exact).

(2): let (i, 0) be a resonance. Then χ_{i+1} = χ_i·(d/a) = 1, so v = x^{k−i−1}y^{i+1} spans H⁰(B, gr_{i+1}). No (i + 1, s) is a resonance, because (a/d)^{p^s} = 1 on T′ would put T′ in the scalars; so H¹(B, gr_{i+1}) = 0. In 0 → gr_i → M_{i+1}/M_{i−1} → gr_{i+1} → 0 the connecting map (Mathlib groupCohomology.δ, computed by groupCohomology.δ₀_apply) sends v to the class of b ↦ b·ṽ − ṽ, whose restriction to U is u(c) ↦ (i + 1)·c·x^{k−i}y^i ≠ 0, as 1 ≤ i + 1 ≤ k ≤ p − 1. Since dim H¹(B, gr_i) ≤ 1 (only s = 0 is a resonance at i), the connecting map is onto, and H¹(B, M_{i+1}/M_{i−1}) = 0 by exactness (groupCohomology.mapShortComplex₁_exact, mapShortComplex₂_exact). Two resonances (i, 0), (i′, 0) have (d/a)^{i′−i} = 1 on T′, so |i′ − i| ≥ 2 and these two-step blocks do not overlap. M is thus filtered by B-modules with vanishing H¹, and H¹(B, M) = 0.
(3) is G7/h1-restriction-injective-for-invertible-index for B ≤ G.

(a): for T′ = {diag(a, a⁻¹)}, χ_i(t) = a^{k−2i} and a/d = a², so (i, s) is a resonance iff k − 2i ≡ 2p^s mod (q − 1). If r ≥ 2 and p ≥ 5, |k − 2i − 2p^s| ≤ (p − 1) + 2p^{r−1} < q − 1, so k − 2i = 2p^s, which forces s = 0 and i = (k − 2)/2 < k. If r = 1, k − 2i ≡ 2 mod (p − 1) with |k − 2i| ≤ p − 1 means k − 2i = 2 or k − 2i = 3 − p; the second has i = k only for k = p − 3 (and i = p − 2 < k for k = p − 1). The index [SL₂(F) : B] = q + 1 is prime to p. (b): χ_i(t) = a^{1−i}d^{i−1} equals a/d on the full torus iff (a/d)^i = 1 for all a, d, iff (p − 1) | i, iff i = 0 (as i ≤ 2 < p − 1); [GL₂(F_p) : B] = p + 1.
acceptance: (a) for F = F_p, p = 5, 7, 11: H¹(SL₂(F_p), Sym^k) = 0 for 0 ≤ k ≤ p − 1, k ≠ p − 3, and the excluded case has H¹ of dimension 1 (finite computation of the cocycle space on generators).
(a) for F = F_{p²}: the Borel subgroups of SL₂(F_25), SL₂(F_49), SL₂(F_121) have H¹ = 0 with coefficients Sym^k for the even k ≤ p − 3 tested (2; 2, 4; 2, 4, 6, 8), including k = p − 3.
(b): H¹(GL₂(F_5), ad⁰) = 0 although H¹(SL₂(F_5), ad⁰) is one-dimensional; and H¹(GL₂(F_5), Sym² ⊗ det¹) ≠ 0, where χ_2 = a·d³ = a/d on F_5^× × F_5^× gives the resonance (2, 0) with i = k.

nodes.title: Verification criteria for adequacy: large characteristic, prime-to-p order, normal subgroups, tensor products, rank two and SL₂(p^r)
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime, k a field of characteristic p and H ⊆ GL_n(k) a finite subgroup; 'adequate' and 'GHT-adequate' are as in G7/adequate-subgroup. (1) (Guralnick–Herzig–Taylor–Thorne, appendix to Thorne 2012, Theorem 9, cited as Theorem A.9) Suppose H acts irreducibly on k̄^n, let H⁺ be the subgroup generated by the elements of p-power order (then k̄^n is a semisimple H⁺-module) and let d be the largest dimension of an irreducible H⁺-submodule of k̄^n. If p ≥ 2(d+1), then H⁰(H, ad⁰) = H¹(H, ad⁰) = H¹(H, k) = 0 and the semisimple elements of H span ad; hence H is adequate. In particular every absolutely irreducible H ⊆ GL_n(k) is adequate if p ≥ 2(n+1) (Thorne 2012, Lemma 2.4(ii); Newton–Thorne 2026, §2: p > 2n+2). (2) If p ∤ #H and H acts absolutely irreducibly, H is adequate (BLGG13 Remark A.1.2; GHTT Lemma 2(i)). (3) If N ⊴ H is adequate and p ∤ [H : N], then H is adequate (BLGG13 Lemma A.1.3); and if H acts irreducibly and some subgroup of H containing a Sylow p-subgroup of H is GHT-adequate on k^n, in particular if H⁺ is, then H is GHT-adequate (GHT17 Remark 6.1). (4) (BLGG13 Lemma A.3.1, Taylor) For a group Γ and representations r_i : Γ → GL_{n_i}(k̄), i = 1, 2, with r₁(Γ) adequate, r₂|_{ker r₁} irreducible and p ∤ #r₂(Γ), the image (r₁ ⊗ r₂)(Γ) is adequate; the same proof shows: if r₁(Γ) satisfies H¹(r₁(Γ), k̄) = 0, H¹(r₁(Γ), ad) = 0 and the spanning condition, so does (r₁ ⊗ r₂)(Γ) (Boxer–Calegari–Gee 2025, proof of Theorem 3.1). (5) (rank two; BLGG13 Proposition A.2.1 as corrected by sourceIssue E754, in agreement with Guralnick–Herzig–Tiep, Corollary 9.5 and Gee–Newton Lemma 3.2.3) If p > 2 and G ⊆ GL₂(F̄_p) is finite and irreducible on F̄_p², then G is adequate unless p = 3 and the image of G in PGL₂(F̄_3) is conjugate to PSL₂(F_3), or p = 5 and that image is conjugate to PSL₂(F_5). (6) (GHT17 Corollary 9.4) A nontrivial absolutely irreducible representation V of SL₂(F_{p^r}) over a field of characteristic p is GHT-adequate unless (i) r = 1 and 1 < dim V = (p ± 1)/2, (ii) p^r ∈ {2, 3, 4} and dim V = p^r, or (iii) p^r = 9 and dim V ∈ {3, 6, 9}.
hypotheses: (1) needs H irreducible and p ≥ 2(d+1) with d computed for H⁺, not for H
(4) needs p ∤ #r₂(Γ) and r₂ irreducible on ker r₁; tensor products of two adequate groups need not be adequate
(5) is for p odd; p = 2 and n = 2 is excluded since then p | n
(6) concerns GHT-adequacy; for p ∤ dim V it is Thorne-adequacy
proofSteps: (1): GHTT Theorem 9. dim V is prime to p (Clifford theory and [CR62, 51.7]); by Proposition 7 (which rests on the classification of finite simple groups) H is r(G(F_p)) for an algebraic group G = G⁰ ⋊ H₀ with G⁰ simply connected semisimple and p ∤ #H₀; H¹(H⁺, Hom(W_i, W_j)) = Ext¹ vanishes by Guralnick 1999, Theorem A, as dim W_i + dim W_j ≤ p − 2; then H¹(H, ad V) = 0 via the index-prime-to-p restriction, and the spanning statement follows from Lemma 3 and Lemma 8 on maximal tori. These two external inputs are recorded as a gap. The 'in particular' is Thorne 2012 Lemma 2.4(ii) with d ≤ n.

(2): BLGG13 Remark A.1.2: (A1) is trivial; p ∤ n by G7/dimension-of-absolutely-irreducible-representations-of-prime-to-p-groups (the source lifts to characteristic 0 and uses that n divides #H); every element is semisimple and spans by Burnside; H¹ vanishes because #H is invertible in k (G7/h1-restriction-injective-for-invertible-index (i)).

(3): BLGG13 Lemma A.1.3 by the inflation–restriction exact sequence (Mathlib groupCohomology.H1InfRes_exact) for N ⊴ H with ad^N = k·1, and GHT17 Remark 6.1 (spanning passes to overgroups; H¹ injects under restriction to a subgroup containing a Sylow p-subgroup, by G7/h1-restriction-injective-for-invertible-index (ii)).

(4): BLGG13 Lemma A.3.1: with H_i = r_i(Γ), K_i = r_i(ker r_{3−i}) and Z the scalars z with (z, z⁻¹) in the image, H/K₂ ≅ H₁/Z; spanning is checked on A₁ ⊗ A₂ using r₂(ker r₁)-spans; the tensor product is Mathlib's Representation.tprod. H¹ by inflation–restriction (Mathlib groupCohomology.H1InfRes_exact for K₂ ⊴ H): H¹(H/K₂, ad(r₁⊗r₂)^{K₂}) = H¹(H₁/Z, ad r₁) = 0 (inflation to H₁ is injective and H¹(H₁, ad r₁) = 0) and H¹(K₂, ad(r₁⊗r₂)) = 0 as p ∤ #K₂ (G7/h1-restriction-injective-for-invertible-index (i)).

(5): BLGG13 Proposition A.2.1 case analysis over Dickson's list (ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations:R01.4/dickson-classification-and-the-dyadic-refinement): p ≥ 7 by (1) with d ≤ 2; prime-to-p projective images by (2); PSL₂/PGL₂(k) with |k| ≥ p² by reduction to SL₂(k) and G7/h1-of-sl2-with-adjoint-coefficients; p = 3 with PGL₂(F_3) or A₅ adequate; p = 3 with PSL₂(F_3) fails (A1); p = 5 with PSL₂(F_5) fails as H¹(SL₂(F_5), ad⁰) ≠ 0. For p = 5 with image PGL₂(F_5): replace G by k^×G and then by GL₂(F_5) (Lemmas A.1.3, A.1.4); H¹(GL₂(F_5), ad⁰) = 0 (G7/h1-of-sl2-with-adjoint-coefficients (b)), so G is adequate — the opposite of BLGG13's Point 5 (E754). Guralnick–Herzig–Tiep, Corollary 9.5 proves the same for every faithful absolutely irreducible representation with projective image PGL₂(p^a), p odd, p^a > 3.

(6): GHT17 Corollary 9.4: r = 1 is [GHT, Cor. 1.4]; for r > 1, Ext¹_G(V,V) = 0 by Andersen–Jørgensen–Landrock [2, Cor. 4.5(a)], H¹(G,k) = 0 as G is perfect and H²(G,k) = 0 unless p^r ∈ {4, 9}; the cases p^r = 4, 9 are computed via tilting modules T(b₀) ⊗ T(b₁)^{(1)}. The AJL Ext computation is not in any library and is recorded as a gap.
acceptance: (1) with n = 2: every irreducible G ⊆ GL₂(F̄_p) is adequate for p ≥ 7 (d ≤ 2 gives p ≥ 6); with n = 4 and H ⊆ GSp₄(k) absolutely irreducible, p ≥ 11 suffices, which is Boxer–Calegari–Gee–Pilloni Lemma 7.5.14.
(5) at p = 5: SL₂(F_5) and every G with projective image PSL₂(F_5) are not adequate; GL₂(F_5) is (H¹(GL₂(F_5), ad⁰) = 0 by the computation recorded in G7/h1-of-sl2-with-adjoint-coefficients).

(6) with V = Sym^{n−1} of the standard representation of SL₂(F_p), n ≤ p: for p ≥ 5, V is GHT-adequate unless n = (p ± 1)/2 (n > 1). For p ≤ 3 case (ii) excludes n = p as well: for p = 3, n = 3 the image A₄ of SL₂(F_3) in GL₃(F̄_3) has only four semisimple elements (1 and three involutions), which cannot span the 9-dimensional M₃; for p = 2, n = 2 the group SL₂(F_2) ≅ S₃ has a quotient of order 2, so H¹(H, k) ≠ 0 and V is not GHT-adequate (part (5) is for p odd and says nothing here). For n = 2 and p odd the exceptions are exactly p = 3 and p = 5, matching (5).

(2) with p odd: the quaternion group Q₈ ⊆ SL₂(F̄_p) acting by its two-dimensional representation is adequate, and so is the image of Q₈ × Q₈ in GL₄(F̄_p) acting on the tensor product (order 32, irreducible); the latter is not enormous (G7/enormous-image-and-its-coefficient-extension-invariance, acceptance), so (2) does not extend to enormous image.

nodes.title: An absolutely irreducible representation of a finite group of order prime to p has dimension prime to p
nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic p > 0, H a finite group with p ∤ #H, and V an absolutely irreducible representation of H over k, of dimension n. Then p ∤ n. Equivalently, for a finite subgroup H ⊆ GL_n(k) of order prime to p that spans M_n(k), the scalar matrices are not of trace zero.
hypotheses: p ∤ #H is needed: SL₂(F_p) acts absolutely irreducibly on Sym^{p−1}(F̄_p²), of dimension p
proofSteps: Extend scalars to an algebraic closure k̄; V ⊗ k̄ is irreducible (R01.1/absolutely-irreducible). The element z = Σ_{h ∈ H} tr(h⁻¹ | V)·h of k̄[H] is central, so it acts on V ⊗ k̄ by a scalar λ (Schur's lemma).

Taking traces: n·λ = Σ_h tr(h⁻¹)·tr(h) = #H, by orthogonality of characters for an irreducible representation over an algebraically closed field in which #H is invertible (Mathlib FDRep.char_orthonormal with V = W). As #H ≠ 0 in k, n ≠ 0 in k.
acceptance: Q₈ ⊆ SL₂(F_p), p odd: n = 2.
Non-example for the hypothesis: SL₂(F_p) on Sym^{p−1} has dimension p.

sources.match: The source's argument (lift to characteristic zero, where the dimension divides the order); the node proves the consequence l ∤ n directly ('characteristiczero' is the text layer's rendering).

nodes.title: The 'enormous' condition for Taylor–Wiles data, its failure when p divides n, and its invariance under coefficient extension
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime, k an algebraic extension of F_p, n ≥ 1, and ad⁰ ⊆ M_n(k) the trace-zero matrices with the conjugation action of GL_n(k) (G7/adjoint-representations). An element h ∈ GL_n(k) is regular semisimple if its characteristic polynomial has n distinct roots in k̄ (equivalently is separable). An absolutely irreducible (R01.1/absolutely-irreducible) subgroup H ⊆ GL_n(k) is enormous over k (Allen et al. 2023, Definition 6.2.29; Definition 6.2.28 in the 2018 arXiv version that Qian cites) if (1) H has no nontrivial quotient of p-power order; (2) H⁰(H, ad⁰) = H¹(H, ad⁰) = 0; (3) for every simple k[H]-submodule W ⊆ ad⁰ there is a regular semisimple h ∈ H with W^h ≠ 0. The condition depends only on the image of H in PGL_n(k). If p | n, no subgroup of GL_n(k) is enormous, because the scalar matrices lie in ad⁰ and are H-invariant. (Lemma 6.2.30) For an algebraic extension k'/k and H ⊆ GL_n(k), H is enormous over k if and only if it is enormous over k'; hence 'enormous' is used without 'over k'. (Remark 6.2.31) If k contains all eigenvalues of all elements of H, H is enormous iff it satisfies Khare–Thorne 2017, Definition 4.10: (1), (2) and (3') for every simple k[H]-submodule W ⊆ ad⁰ there are h ∈ H with n distinct eigenvalues in k and an eigenvalue α of h with tr(e_{h,α}W) ≠ 0. Relation with adequacy: if k contains all eigenvalues of the elements of a finite enormous H, then H is adequate (Gee–Newton, Remark 3.2.2, via bigness); for n = 2 and p odd, enormous and adequate coincide for irreducible finite H (Gee–Newton, Lemma 3.2.3). Enormous is not a synonym for adequate: an adequate group need not contain any regular semisimple element (acceptance: an example in GL₄).
hypotheses: H must be absolutely irreducible as part of the definition, not merely irreducible
condition (3) requires h to be regular semisimple; dropping regularity gives a different condition
the condition cannot hold when p divides n; the source says so explicitly
the equivalence with Khare–Thorne Definition 4.10 holds under the hypothesis that k contains all eigenvalues of the elements of H
in the applications the group is the image of ρ̄ restricted to G_{F(ζ_p)}, not the image of ρ̄ itself
H need not be finite in the definition, although in applications it is the image of a continuous representation into GL_n of a finite field

Khare–Thorne Definition 4.10 and Gee–Newton Definition 3.2.1 do not put absolute irreducibility into the definition (Gee–Newton assume H irreducible, Khare–Thorne nothing); it follows from (3′) for n ≥ 2, because then the projections e_{h,α} of regular semisimple h ∈ H span M_n(k). Khare–Thorne print 'α is an eigenvalue of H' for 'of h' (sourceIssue E780).
H⁰ and H¹ are Mathlib's groupCohomology.H0 and groupCohomology.H1 of the abstract group H (k, H and ad⁰ in one universe; no topology on H).
proofSteps: Lemma 6.2.30 (Allen et al.): only (3) needs attention, and it is equivalent to: for all nonzero k[H]-submodules W ⊆ ad⁰ there is a regular semisimple h ∈ H with W^h ≠ 0. In that form enormity over k' implies enormity over k.

Conversely, the property V^h = 0 is closed under direct sums and quotients (V^h ≠ 0 iff the coinvariants V_h ≠ 0, since dim ker(h − 1) = dim coker(h − 1)). For V ⊆ ad⁰ ⊗_k k′, σhv = hσv for σ ∈ Gal(k′/k) since H ⊆ GL_n(k), so V^h ≠ 0 iff (σV)^h ≠ 0. Let W′ be a simple k′[H]-submodule of ad⁰ ⊗_k k′. The submodule generated by all σW′ is stable under H and Gal(k′/k), hence by G7/galois-descent-of-stable-subspaces (k′/k is Galois, k being algebraic over F_p) it is W ⊗_k k′ for a nonzero k[H]-submodule W ⊆ ad⁰, which does not depend on h; and for each fixed h ∈ H, (W′)^h = 0 implies (W ⊗_k k′)^h = 0. Condition (3) applied to a simple submodule of W gives a regular semisimple h with W^h ≠ 0, hence (W ⊗_k k′)^h ≠ 0, hence (W′)^h ≠ 0. This is the printed argument, with h fixed in its sentence 'In particular …'. Condition (1) does not involve k. Condition (2) is insensitive to k′/k by G7/vanishing-of-h0-and-h1-under-extension-of-the-coefficient-field (parts (1)–(3), which do not need H finite), and absolute irreducibility is invariant (R01.1/absolutely-irreducible).

Projective invariance: the conjugation action on ad⁰ factors through the image P of H in PGL_n(k); (1) passes between H and P because the kernel Z = H ∩ k^× (the scalars are the centre of GL_n: Mathlib Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup.center_eq_range_scalar) consists of elements of order prime to p (k^× has no p-torsion); (2) by inflation–restriction (Mathlib groupCohomology.H1InfRes_exact): Z acts trivially on ad⁰ and is a torsion group without elements of order p, so H¹(Z, ad⁰) = Hom(Z, ad⁰) = 0 (ad⁰ is killed by p) and H^i(P, ad⁰) = H^i(H, ad⁰) for i = 0, 1; (3) is unchanged since regularity and fixed vectors are unchanged by scalars.

Remark 6.2.31: with all eigenvalues in k, a regular semisimple h is diagonalisable over k with one-dimensional eigenspaces, and W^h ≠ 0 iff tr(e_{h,α}W) ≠ 0 for some eigenvalue α (ad^h is the span of the e_{h,α}; its orthogonal complement for the H-invariant trace pairing on ad is (h − 1)·ad; h acts semisimply on ad, so W = W^h ⊕ (h − 1)W, and W ⊄ (h − 1)·ad iff W^h ≠ 0); compare Khare–Thorne Definition 4.10.

Enormous ⇒ adequate (k containing eigenvalues): Gee–Newton Remark 3.2.2 — enormous is big in the sense of CHT08 Definition 2.5.1 (a regular semisimple element has multiplicity-one eigenvalues), and big ⇒ adequate (Thorne 2012 Lemma 2.4(i)); (1) gives H¹(H, k) = 0. For n = 2, Gee–Newton Lemma 3.2.3: if tr(e_{h,α}W) ≠ 0 for W ⊆ ad⁰ then h has distinct eigenvalues (else e_{h,α} = 1 and tr W = 0).
acceptance: SL₂(F_p) ⊆ GL₂(F_p) is enormous for every p ≥ 7: SL₂(F_p) is perfect (Mathlib Matrix.SL2.commutator_eq_top, as F_p has an element a with a² ≠ 1), ad⁰ = Sym² ⊗ det⁻¹ is absolutely irreducible with H⁰ = 0, H¹(SL₂(F_p), ad⁰) = 0 for p ≠ 5 (Darmon–Diamond–Taylor Lemma 2.48; G7/h1-of-sl2-with-adjoint-coefficients), and h = diag(a, a⁻¹) with a² ≠ 1 is regular semisimple and fixes diag(1, −1) ∈ ad⁰.

SL₂(F_5) is not enormous (H¹(SL₂(F_5), ad⁰) is one-dimensional); SL₂(F_3) is not enormous (quotient of order 3, although H⁰ = H¹ = 0 for ad⁰); SL₂(F_2) is not enormous (2 | 2). GL₂(F_5) is enormous (H¹(GL₂(F_5), ad⁰) = 0, no quotient of order 5), so a subgroup of an enormous group need not be enormous.
For n = p: the scalar matrix 1 has trace p = 0, so 1 ∈ ad⁰ is H-invariant and (2) fails for every H ⊆ GL_p(k).

Not merely a synonym for adequacy: for p odd the image H of Q₈ × Q₈ in GL₄(F̄_p) acting on the tensor product of two copies of the two-dimensional representation has order 32, is irreducible and hence adequate (G7/adequacy-criteria (2)), but every element g ⊗ h has repeated eigenvalues (products of {±1} or {±i} with {±1} or {±i}), so H has no regular semisimple element and is not enormous.
Lemma 6.2.30 check: SL₂(F_7) is enormous over F_7 and over F_49.

nodes.title: Galois descent for stable subspaces of V ⊗_k k′
nodes.statement: Let k′/k be a Galois extension of fields (algebraic, possibly infinite), V a k-vector space, and W′ ⊆ V ⊗_k k′ a k′-subspace with (1 ⊗ σ)(W′) ⊆ W′ for every σ ∈ Gal(k′/k). Then W′ = W ⊗_k k′ for the k-subspace W = W′ ∩ V (V embedded by v ↦ v ⊗ 1). If a group H acts k-linearly on V and W′ is stable under H (acting through V), then W is H-stable; and W ≠ 0 if W′ ≠ 0.
hypotheses: k′/k must be Galois: the proof uses that the elements of k′ fixed by Gal(k′/k) are those of k
every algebraic extension of an algebraic extension of F_p is Galois, which is the case used
proofSteps: W ⊗_k k′ ⊆ W′ is clear. Let X′ be the image of W′ in (V/W) ⊗_k k′; it is stable under Gal(k′/k). If X′ ≠ 0, choose 0 ≠ x′ = Σ_{j=1}^{m} ū_j ⊗ a_j ∈ X′ with the ū_j ∈ V/W linearly independent over k, m minimal and a_1 = 1.

For σ ∈ Gal(k′/k), σx′ − x′ = Σ_{j≥2} ū_j ⊗ (σa_j − a_j) ∈ X′ has fewer terms, hence is 0, so σa_j = a_j for all σ and all j; the fixed elements are in k (Mathlib InfiniteGalois.mem_bot_iff_fixed), so x′ = ū ⊗ 1 with 0 ≠ ū ∈ V/W.

Lift: some w′ ∈ W′ maps to ū ⊗ 1, i.e. w′ − u ⊗ 1 ∈ W ⊗ k′ ⊆ W′ for a u ∈ V lifting ū; then u ⊗ 1 ∈ W′, so u ∈ W and ū = 0, a contradiction. Hence X′ = 0 and W′ ⊆ W ⊗ k′. H-stability of W = W′ ∩ V is immediate.
acceptance: k = F_3, k′ = F_9 = F_3(i), V = k², W′ the line spanned by (1, i): it is not stable under the Frobenius (its conjugate is the line of (1, −i)) and W′ ∩ V = 0; the sum W′ + σW′ = V ⊗ k′ is stable and descends to W = V.

sources.match: The use: a submodule stable under H and Gal(k′/k) 'thus (by descent) has the form W ⊗_k k′' (the text layer renders the primes as 0).

nodes.title: Enormous subgroups of GL_n(O) in characteristic zero (Newton–Thorne) and the Zariski-closure criterion
nodes.statement: Let E/Q_p be a finite extension with ring of integers O, n ≥ 1, and W_E = M_n(E) = ad ⊗_O E with H acting by conjugation. A subgroup H ⊆ GL_n(O) is enormous in the characteristic-zero sense (Newton–Thorne 2023, Definition 2.23) if for every simple E[H]-submodule V ⊆ W_E there are h ∈ H with n distinct eigenvalues in E and an eigenvalue α ∈ E of h with tr(e_{h,α}V) ≠ 0, where e_{h,α} is the h-equivariant projection onto the α-eigenspace. No vanishing of cohomology and no p-power-quotient condition is imposed, and the whole of W_E (not its trace-zero part) is tested. Facts: (Lemma 2.25) such H acts absolutely irreducibly on E^n, so H⁰(H, W⁰_E) = 0. (Lemma 2.28) Suppose every h ∈ H has characteristic polynomial split over E (§2.5 of the source also fixes H ⊆ GL_n(O) compact; the proof uses neither the compactness of H nor the closedness of H′ in (1), and both are dropped here). (1) If a closed subgroup H' ⊆ H is enormous, so is H. (2) If the identity component G° of the Zariski closure G ⊆ GL_n of H (G7/zariski-closure-and-monodromy-groups) contains regular semisimple elements and acts absolutely irreducibly on E^n, then H is enormous. Newton–Thorne 2026 (proof of Lemma 4.7) applies (2) through: if the derived subgroup G¹ of G° contains regular semisimple elements and acts absolutely irreducibly, and G¹ lies in the Zariski closure of H, then H is enormous. This notion is distinct from the residual notion of G7/enormous-image-and-its-coefficient-extension-invariance: it lives over a characteristic-zero field, has no cohomological conditions, and neither notion is deduced from the other.
hypotheses: E has characteristic zero; the residual notion is a different definition
Lemma 2.28 needs the characteristic polynomials of elements of H to split over E (enlarge E if necessary)
regular semisimple elements of G° (an algebraic group over E), not merely of H, are required in Lemma 2.28(2)

Lean carrier: 'h has n distinct eigenvalues in E' means that Matrix.charpoly h splits over E with simple roots (Polynomial.Separable), and e_{h,α} is the projection onto Module.End.maxGenEigenspace h α along the other eigenspaces (for such h the generalised eigenspaces are the eigenspaces).
proofSteps: Lemma 2.25: if U = {u ∈ W_E : tr(hu) = 0 for all h ∈ H} is nonzero, a simple submodule V of U violates the definition (tr(e_{h,α}V) = 0 since e_{h,α} is a polynomial in h); so H spans W_E and acts absolutely irreducibly by Burnside's theorem.

Lemma 2.28(1) is immediate from the definition. (2): reduce to G = G°; G(E) spans W_E by absolute irreducibility; the regular semisimple locus G^reg is a nonempty Zariski-open subset and H^reg = H ∩ G^reg is Zariski dense in G; if tr(hv) = 0 for all h ∈ H^reg then tr(gv) = 0 for all g ∈ G, so v = 0. For h ∈ H^reg, h = Σ_α α·e_{h,α} with all α ∈ E by hypothesis, so tr(hv) ≠ 0 gives tr(e_{h,α}v) ≠ 0 for some α. The reduction to G = G° replaces H by H ∩ G°(E), of finite index in H with Zariski closure G°, and uses (1).

Newton–Thorne 2026, Lemma 4.7: G¹ ⊆ Zariski closure of ρ(G_{K(ζ_{p^∞})}) (passage to derived subgroups commutes with Zariski closure: quoted from Newton–Thorne 2023, Example 2.29, who cite Borel, Linear algebraic groups, Ch. I, §2.1; the fact is taken from that quotation) and G° and G¹ have the same invariant subspaces, so Lemma 2.28 applies to ρ(G_{K(ζ_{p^∞})}).
acceptance: Newton–Thorne 2023 Example 2.29: for π regular algebraic cuspidal on GL₂ over a totally real or CM field with Sym²π cuspidal, a model of Sym^{n−1} r_{π,ι} has ρ(G_{F(ζ_{p^∞})}) enormous (the Zariski closure contains Sym^{n−1}(SL₂), which has regular semisimple elements and acts irreducibly).

A finite irreducible subgroup with no element of n distinct eigenvalues (the image of Q₈ × Q₈ on the four-dimensional tensor product, now over a p-adic field containing i) is not enormous in this sense; its Zariski closure is finite and contains no regular semisimple element.

nodes.title: Symmetric powers of groups containing SL₂(F_l) are enormous, and the Galois-theoretic consequence after restriction to F'(ζ_l)
nodes.statement: (1) (Gee–Newton, Lemma 3.2.5; Clozel–Harris–Taylor Corollary 2.5.4 with the corrected bound) Let n ≥ 2, p a prime with p > 2n + 1, k an algebraic extension of F_p, k' ⊆ k a finite subfield and H ⊆ GL_n(k) with k^× · Sym^{n−1}GL₂(k') ⊇ H ⊇ Sym^{n−1}SL₂(k'), where Sym^{n−1} : GL₂ → GL_n is the symmetric power of G7/symmetric-and-exterior-powers in the monomial basis. Then H is enormous. (2) (Allen et al. 2023, Lemma 7.1.4, with the codomain corrected to GL_n, sourceIssue E751) If n ≥ 2, l > 2n + 1 and H ⊆ GL₂(F̄_l) is a finite subgroup containing SL₂(F_l), then Sym^{n−1}H ⊆ GL_n(F̄_l) is enormous. (3) (Allen et al. 2023, Lemma 7.1.6(2); Qian 2023, Lemma 2.6(1)) Let F/Q be finite with normal closure F̃, m ≥ 1, l > 2m + 3 a prime, r̄ : G_F → GL₂(F̄_l) continuous with r̄(G_{F̃}) ⊇ SL₂(F_l), and F'/F a finite extension linearly disjoint from F̄^{ker r̄} over F. Then (Sym^m r̄)(G_{F'(ζ_l)}) is enormous. Qian's form (n = m + 1, l > 2n + 5) is the special case with a stronger bound; for n = 1 the image is trivial in GL₁ and enormous. (4) (Gee–Newton, Lemma 3.2.4) If n > 2, p > n, k' ⊆ k is a finite subfield and k^× · GL_n(k') ⊇ H ⊇ SL_n(k'), then H is enormous.
hypotheses: the bound is p > 2n + 1 (l > 2m + 3 for Sym^m); Clozel–Harris–Taylor print l > 2n − 1, which fails for n = 2, l = 5 (sourceIssue E756)
(3) needs SL₂(F_l) ⊆ r̄(G_{F̃}) with F̃ the normal closure, and linear disjointness from the field cut out by r̄ itself, not by ad r̄
the subgroup in (3) is the image of G_{F'(ζ_l)}, not of G_{F'}
proofSteps: (1), condition (2) of enormity: as SL₂(k')-modules ad Sym^{n−1} ≅ ⊕_{i=0}^{n−1} Sym^{2i} ⊗ det^{−i} (G7/mod-p-clebsch-gordan-decompositions (d), valid as 2n − 2 < p), each Sym^{2i} irreducible (G7/adjoint-invariants-of-symmetric-powers (a)); so H⁰(Sym^{n−1}SL₂(k'), ad⁰) = 0, and H¹(SL₂(k'), Sym^{2i}) = 0 for 1 ≤ i ≤ n − 1 because 2i ≤ 2n − 2 < p − 3 (G7/h1-of-sl2-with-adjoint-coefficients (c)); pass from Sym^{n−1}SL₂(k') to H: H¹(H, ad⁰) → H¹(H ∩ k^×·Sym^{n−1}SL₂(k'), ad⁰) is injective as the index divides 2 (G7/h1-restriction-injective-for-invertible-index), and inflation–restriction (Mathlib groupCohomology.H1InfRes_exact) removes the scalars, which have order prime to p and act trivially on ad⁰. Condition (1): PSL₂(k') is simple (Mathlib Matrix.ProjectiveSpecialLinearGroup.rank_two_simple, as #k′ ≥ 5) and the quotient of H by Sym^{n−1}SL₂(k')·(scalars) has order dividing #k'^× · 2. Condition (3): Clozel–Harris–Taylor Lemma 2.5.2 — the diagonal torus generator t of SL₂(k') has the n eigenvalues a^{n−1−2j} on Sym^{n−1}, a a generator of k′^×, which are distinct because 2(n − 1) < p − 1 ≤ #k′ − 1 (n < p alone would not suffice: for p = 7, n = 4 the eigenvalues a^{3} and a^{−3} coincide) and each Sym^{2i} meets the t-fixed part D = ⊕ Hom(V_j, V_j) in a line (Gee–Newton: these eigenspaces are one-dimensional, so t is regular semisimple).

(2): Dickson (ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations:R01.4/dickson-classification-and-the-dyadic-refinement): the image of H in PGL₂(F̄_l) is conjugate to PSL₂(k) or PGL₂(k) for a finite k ⊇ F_l, so F̄_l^× Sym^{n−1}GL₂(k) ⊇ Sym^{n−1}H ⊇ Sym^{n−1}SL₂(k), and (1) applies with k' = k.

(3): linear disjointness gives r̄(G_{F'}) = r̄(G_F) ⊇ r̄(G_{F̃}) ⊇ SL₂(F_l); SL₂(F_l) is perfect for l ≥ 5 (Mathlib Matrix.SL2.commutator_eq_top) and Gal(F'(ζ_l)/F') is abelian, so r̄(G_{F'(ζ_l)}) ⊇ SL₂(F_l) (ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations:R01.4/restriction-to-the-cyclotomic-field); apply (2) with n = m + 1, l > 2n + 1 = 2m + 3.

(4): Gee–Newton Lemma 3.2.4 from the proof of Clozel–Harris–Taylor Lemma 2.5.6 (bigness of groups between SL_n(k') and k^×GL_n(k')), plus a regular semisimple element of SL_n(k'): the companion matrix of X^n + (−1)^n, which has n distinct roots as p > n.
acceptance: n = 2, (2): every finite H ⊆ GL₂(F̄_l) containing SL₂(F_l) is enormous for l ≥ 7; for l = 5 the bound l > 5 fails and indeed SL₂(F_5) is not enormous (H¹(SL₂(F_5), ad⁰) ≠ 0), which shows the printed Clozel–Harris–Taylor bound l > 2n − 1 = 3 is too weak.
n = 3, l = 11 (> 7): Sym²(SL₂(F_11)) ≅ SO₃-image in GL₃(F_11) is enormous; ad⁰ Sym² = Sym² ⊕ Sym⁴ (twists) and H¹(SL₂(F_11), Sym^{2i}) = 0 for i = 1, 2 since 2, 4 ≠ 11 − 3.
(3) for an elliptic curve E/Q without CM and l ≥ 7 with r̄_{E,l}(G_Q) = GL₂(F_l), F = F' = Q, m = 1: r̄_{E,l}(G_{Q(ζ_l)}) = SL₂(F_l) is enormous.

nodes.title: H¹(SL₂(F), ad⁰) vanishes unless #F = 5, and the symmetric-power vanishing behind the bound p > 2n + 1
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field of odd characteristic p and ad⁰ = End⁰(F²) = sl₂(F) with the conjugation action. (a) (Darmon–Diamond–Taylor, Lemma 2.48) If #F ≠ 5 then H¹(SL₂(F), ad⁰) = 0; also H⁰(SL₂(F), ad⁰) = 0. (b) For F = F_5, H¹(SL₂(F_5), ad⁰) is one-dimensional over F_5, while H¹(GL₂(F_5), ad⁰) = 0 and H¹(GL₂(F_5), ad⁰ ⊗ det²) is one-dimensional; consequently H¹(G, ad⁰) = 0 for every G ⊆ GL₂(F̄_5) whose image in PGL₂(F̄_5) is conjugate to PGL₂(F_5), and H¹(G, ad⁰) ≠ 0 when that image is PSL₂(F_5). (c) (input to Clozel–Harris–Taylor Corollary 2.5.4, with the corrected bound) If n ≥ 2, p > 2n + 1 and F ⊇ F_p is finite, then H¹(SL₂(F), Sym^{2i}(F̄_p²)) = 0 for 1 ≤ i ≤ n − 1. In particular H¹(SL₂(F_p), ad⁰) = 0 for p ≥ 7 is the case n = 2 of (c) and of (a).
hypotheses: p odd; for p = 2, ad⁰ contains the scalars
#F = 5 is a genuine exception in (a), not an artefact of the proof

(c) for F = F_p needs 2i ≠ p − 3 for all i ≤ n − 1, which p > 2n + 1 guarantees: H¹(SL₂(F_p), Sym^{p−3}) is one-dimensional, and H¹(SL₂(F_p), Sym^a) = 0 for the other 0 ≤ a ≤ p − 1 (checked for p = 5, 7, 11). For F ≠ F_p the argument gives the vanishing for 2i = p − 3 as well.
proofSteps: (a): Darmon–Diamond–Taylor Lemma 2.48, with H¹ Mathlib's groupCohomology.H1 of the finite group SL₂(F) (Mathlib Matrix.SpecialLinearGroup). H⁰ = 0 because ad⁰ ≅ Sym² is irreducible and nontrivial for p odd. As SL₂(F)-modules ad⁰ ≅ Sym²(F²), so for p ≥ 5 and #F ≠ 5 the vanishing is G7/h1-of-borel-subgroups-with-symmetric-power-coefficients (a) with k = 2 (k = p − 3 only for p = 5, where #F ≥ 25 is assumed). For p = 3: if #F = 3, Sym² is free over F_3[U] for the unipotent subgroup U of order 3 (dimension 3, one Jordan block), so H¹(U, Sym²) = 0 (Mathlib Rep.FiniteCyclicGroup.groupCohomologyIsoOdd: H¹ is the kernel of the norm modulo the image of u − 1, and the norm (u − 1)² has kernel (u − 1)·Sym²), and H¹(SL₂(F_3), ad⁰) ↪ H¹(U, ad⁰) by G7/h1-restriction-injective-for-invertible-index; if #F = 3^r with r ≥ 3, part (2) of the Borel lemma applies with k = 2, since |2 − 2i − 2·3^s| ≤ 2 + 2·3^{r−1} < 3^r − 1 leaves only the resonance (0, 0). If #F = 9 there is the second resonance (2, 1) (2 − 4 ≡ 2·3 mod 8), with s ≠ 0, and the Borel lemma does not apply: Darmon–Diamond–Taylor indicate that the corresponding class in H¹(B, M₃/M₂) maps injectively to H²(B, M₂) under the connecting homomorphism; that check is not written out by them or here; H¹(SL₂(F_9), Sym²) = 0 is confirmed by a finite computation of the cocycle space.

(b): H¹(GL₂(F_5), ad⁰) = 0 is G7/h1-of-borel-subgroups-with-symmetric-power-coefficients (b). For any G with U ⊆ G ⊆ GL₂(F_p) and M = Sym^k ⊗ det^j, k ≤ p − 2: H¹(G, M) ↪ H¹(U, M) (G7/h1-restriction-injective-for-invertible-index, p ∤ [G : U]), and H¹(U, M) ≅ M/(u − 1)M is one-dimensional (Rep.FiniteCyclicGroup.groupCohomologyIsoOdd; the norm (u − 1)^{p−1} vanishes on M); so dim H¹ ≤ 1 for SL₂(F_5), for {det = ±1} and for GL₂(F_5) with coefficients ad⁰ ⊗ det². That these three are exactly one-dimensional is Cline–Parshall–Scott, Table 4.5 for SL₂(F_5) (cited by Darmon–Diamond–Taylor and by BLGG13, Point 5), and in each case a finite linear-algebra check of the cocycle condition on generators (dim Z¹ = 4, dim B¹ = 3). The same finite check gives dim H¹(SL₂(F_p), ad⁰) = 0, 1, 0, 0, 0 for p = 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 and dim H¹(GL₂(F_5), ad⁰ ⊗ det^j) = 0, 0, 1, 0 for j = 0, 1, 2, 3. The PGL₂(F_5) statement follows by replacing G with k^×G and then with GL₂(F_5) (index prime to 5: G7/h1-restriction-injective-for-invertible-index; scalars: inflation–restriction, Mathlib groupCohomology.H1InfRes_exact).

(c): G7/h1-of-borel-subgroups-with-symmetric-power-coefficients (a) with k = 2i: as p > 2n + 1 gives 2 ≤ k ≤ 2n − 2 ≤ p − 5, k ≠ p − 3 and the hypothesis holds for every finite F ⊇ F_p. This is Darmon–Diamond–Taylor's method for Lemma 2.48. Clozel–Harris–Taylor instead cite Cline–Parshall–Scott, Lemma 2.7(c), with the printed hypothesis l > n + 1, which is too weak (it would include n = 2, l = 5, contradicting (b)). For F = F_p and k = p − 3 the lemma does not apply (the resonance (k, 0) has i = k) and the class survives; for F ≠ F_p it applies to k = p − 3 as well, so H¹(SL₂(F), Sym^{p−3}) = 0 there.
acceptance: Computed: dim H¹(SL₂(F_p), ad⁰) = 0, 1, 0, 0, 0 for p = 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, matching (a) and the exception p = 5 that Calegari–Dimitrov–Tang's proof of Lemma 4.5.6 excludes.
Computed: H¹(GL₂(F_5), ad⁰) = 0 but H¹(GL₂(F_5), ad⁰ ⊗ det²) ≠ 0, so the group GL₂(F_5) is adequate and enormous while SL₂(F_5) is neither.
For p = 2, SL₂(F_2) ≅ S₃ acting on the trace-zero matrices (which contain the scalars) has H⁰ and H¹ both one-dimensional, so the odd-characteristic hypothesis is needed.

For p = 5, 7, 11 and 0 ≤ a ≤ p − 1, H¹(SL₂(F_p), Sym^a(F_p²)) is one-dimensional for a = p − 3 and zero otherwise (finite linear algebra on the cocycle condition; for a ≤ p − 2 the vanishing also follows from the weight computation of (b): diag(z, z⁻¹) acts on H¹(U, Sym^a) through z^{−(a+2)}). So (c) holds for F = F_p, p ≤ 11, and the bound p > 2n + 1 is sharp over F_p (n = (p − 1)/2 gives 2(n − 1) = p − 3). Over F_{p²}, p = 5, 7, 11, the Borel subgroup has H¹ = 0 with coefficients Sym^{p−3}.

nodes.title: Mod p Clebsch–Gordan decompositions: V ⊗ Sym^{r−1}V, the two-constituent congruence for Sym^{p+r−1}V, and End(Sym^{n−1}V)
nodes.statement: Let k be a field, Γ a group and V a two-dimensional representation of Γ over k; Sym^a is G7/symmetric-and-exterior-powers, det = ∧²V, and (·)^ss is R01.1/semisimplification. (a) (Newton–Thorne 2026, (1.3)) If r ≥ 2 and r is invertible in k (in characteristic p: p ∤ r, in particular 1 < r < p), then V ⊗ Sym^{r−1}V ≅ Sym^rV ⊕ (det ⊗ Sym^{r−2}V) as representations of Γ; for r = 1, V ⊗ Sym⁰V ≅ V. (b) (Newton–Thorne 2026, (1.1); Clozel–Thorne 2017, (1.1) for p = 7, r = 2, and proof of Theorem 6.2 for r = 2, general l) Let k ⊇ F_p be perfect, 0 < r < p, and let Frob V be the coefficient Frobenius twist of V (R01.1/coefficient-frobenius-twist: matrix entries raised to the p-th power; for a Galois representation, the action of an arithmetic Frobenius lift φ_p on coefficients). Then (Sym^{p+r−1}V)^ss ≅ (det^{⊗r} ⊗ Sym^{p−r−1}V)^ss ⊕ (Frob V ⊗ Sym^{r−1}V)^ss; this is an identity after semisimplification only. (c) (Boxer–Calegari–Gee 2025, proof of Theorem 2.1) For every n ≥ 1, (End(Sym^{n−1}V))^ss ≅ ⊕_{i=0}^{n−1} (Sym^{2i}V ⊗ det^{−i})^ss. (d) (Clozel–Harris–Taylor, proof of Lemma 2.5.2, there for Γ = SL₂(F_l)) If char k = 0 or char k = p > 2n − 2, then for every Γ and V, End(Sym^{n−1}V) ≅ ⊕_{i=0}^{n−1} Sym^{2i}V ⊗ det^{−i} as representations of Γ, not only after semisimplification; more generally Sym^aV ⊗ Sym^bV ≅ ⊕_{i=0}^{min(a,b)} det^{⊗i} ⊗ Sym^{a+b−2i}V whenever (a + b)! is invertible in k. (Irreducibility of the summands is a separate statement, about groups containing SL₂(F_p), and is not part of (d).)
hypotheses: (a) needs r invertible in k; it is a genuine isomorphism
(b) is only an isomorphism of semisimplifications; Sym^{p+r−1}V is in general a non-split extension
(b) uses the coefficient Frobenius twist, not restriction to a decomposition group or a Frobenius element of Γ
(c) holds for all n after semisimplification; (d) needs p > 2n − 2
proofSteps: (a) is G7/pieri-splitting-for-symmetric-powers (Euler's identity m ∘ Δ = r and the map det ⊗ Sym^{r−2}V → ker m).

(b): by R01.1/brauer-nesbitt it suffices that both sides have the same characteristic polynomial for each γ ∈ Γ. If γ has eigenvalues a, b on V (in k̄), Sym^{p+r−1}V has eigenvalues a^i b^{p+r−1−i}, 0 ≤ i ≤ p+r−1; det^r ⊗ Sym^{p−r−1}V contributes the exponents r ≤ i ≤ p − 1, and Frob V ⊗ Sym^{r−1}V (eigenvalues a^p, b^p on Frob V) contributes i = p + j and i = j for 0 ≤ j ≤ r − 1; the multisets agree.

(c): same method: End(Sym^{n−1}V) = Sym^{n−1}V ⊗ (Sym^{n−1}V)^∨ has eigenvalues (a/b)^m with multiplicity n − |m| for |m| ≤ n − 1, and ⊕_i Sym^{2i}V ⊗ det^{−i} has eigenvalues (a/b)^m, |m| ≤ i, again with multiplicity n − |m|.

(d) is G7/tensor-products-of-symmetric-powers (induction from (a) and Krull–Schmidt; Clozel–Harris–Taylor use Serre's theorem on tensor products of small semisimple modules instead, which is not needed). Remark on (b): if Γ acts through SL₂(F_p) then Frob V ≅ V and Frob V ⊗ V ≅ Sym²V ⊕ det for p odd, so the Frobenius-twisted constituent of (b) is then reducible.
acceptance: Clozel–Thorne (1.1): p = 7, r = 2 gives Sym⁸V ~ (Frob V ⊗ V) ⊕ det² ⊗ Sym⁴V, dimensions 9 = 4 + 5.
(a) with r = 2: V ⊗ V ≅ Sym²V ⊕ det for p odd; for p = 2 this fails (V ⊗ V is not semisimple for SL₂(F_2) acting on F̄_2², the case r = p excluded by the hypothesis).
(c) with n = 2: End(V)^ss ≅ 1 ⊕ (Sym²V ⊗ det⁻¹)^ss, i.e. ad = k ⊕ ad⁰ after semisimplification, which is an honest splitting exactly when p ≠ 2.

nodes.title: V ⊗ Sym^{r−1}V ≅ Sym^rV ⊕ det ⊗ Sym^{r−2}V for r invertible
nodes.statement: Let k be a field, Γ a group and V a two-dimensional representation of Γ over k, with det = ∧²V. If r ≥ 2 and r is invertible in k, then V ⊗ Sym^{r−1}V ≅ Sym^rV ⊕ (det ⊗ Sym^{r−2}V) as representations of Γ; for r = 1, V ⊗ Sym⁰V ≅ V. The isomorphism is natural in V: it is given by the multiplication m : V ⊗ Sym^{r−1}V → Sym^rV, split by r⁻¹·Δ with Δ(F) = x ⊗ ∂_xF + y ⊗ ∂_yF, and by the map det ⊗ Sym^{r−2}V → ker m, (x ∧ y) ⊗ G ↦ x ⊗ yG − y ⊗ xG.
hypotheses: r must be invertible in k: for k of characteristic 2 and r = 2, V ⊗ V ≇ Sym²V ⊕ det for SL₂(F_2) acting on F̄_2²
V has rank exactly two
proofSteps: Δ : Sym^rV → V ⊗ Sym^{r−1}V is the polarisation map (the component of the comultiplication of the symmetric algebra, G7/symmetric-and-exterior-powers); it is natural in V, hence Γ-equivariant, and m ∘ Δ = r·id (Euler's identity on monomials). So V ⊗ Sym^{r−1}V = Δ(Sym^rV) ⊕ ker m.

The map det ⊗ Sym^{r−2}V → V ⊗ Sym^{r−1}V is the composite ∧²V ⊗ Sym^{r−2}V → V ⊗ V ⊗ Sym^{r−2}V → V ⊗ Sym^{r−1}V, natural in V; it is injective (x ⊗ yG = y ⊗ xG forces G = 0) and lands in ker m; dim ker m = 2r − (r + 1) = r − 1 = dim(det ⊗ Sym^{r−2}V).
acceptance: r = 2, p odd: V ⊗ V ≅ Sym²V ⊕ det.
Failure for r = p = 2: for S₃ = SL₂(F_2) on V = F̄_2², V ⊗ V ≅ V ⊕ P(1) with P(1) the non-split projective cover of the trivial module, whereas Sym²V ⊕ det ≅ V ⊕ 1 ⊕ 1 is semisimple.

nodes.title: Sym^aV ⊗ Sym^bV ≅ ⊕ det^i ⊗ Sym^{a+b−2i}V when (a + b)! is invertible
nodes.statement: Let k be a field, Γ a group and V a two-dimensional representation of Γ over k, det = ∧²V, with symmetric powers as in G7/symmetric-and-exterior-powers. If a ≥ b ≥ 0 and (a + b)! is invertible in k (char k = 0 or char k > a + b), then Sym^aV ⊗ Sym^bV ≅ ⊕_{i=0}^{b} det^{⊗i} ⊗ Sym^{a+b−2i}V as representations of Γ. Consequently, for n ≥ 1 with (2n − 2)! invertible in k (char k = 0 or char k > 2n − 2), End(Sym^{n−1}V) ≅ ⊕_{i=0}^{n−1} Sym^{2i}V ⊗ det^{−i} as representations of Γ, not only after semisimplification. Nothing is assumed about Γ or about the image of Γ in GL(V).
hypotheses: (a + b)! invertible is needed: End(V) for p = 2 = a + b is not k ⊕ ad⁰ as a representation of SL₂(F_2)
the statement is an isomorphism of representations, obtained by cancellation, and no explicit isomorphism is claimed
proofSteps: Induction on b for all a ≥ b with (a + b)! invertible; b = 0 is trivial and b = 1 is G7/pieri-splitting-for-symmetric-powers with r = a + 1.

For b ≥ 2: the Pieri splitting with r = b and with r = a + 1 gives Sym^a ⊗ V ⊗ Sym^{b−1} ≅ (Sym^a ⊗ Sym^b) ⊕ det ⊗ (Sym^a ⊗ Sym^{b−2}) and ≅ (Sym^{a+1} ⊗ Sym^{b−1}) ⊕ det ⊗ (Sym^{a−1} ⊗ Sym^{b−1}). By the induction hypothesis for (a + 1, b − 1), (a − 1, b − 1) and (a, b − 2), the second expression is ⊕_{i=0}^{b−1} det^i ⊗ Sym^{a+b−2i} ⊕ ⊕_{i=1}^{b} det^i ⊗ Sym^{a+b−2i}, and the last summand of the first is ⊕_{i=1}^{b−1} det^i ⊗ Sym^{a+b−2i}. Every integer inverted is at most a + b.

Cancellation: finite-dimensional representations of Γ over k are modules of finite length over k[Γ], so each of A, B, C is a finite direct sum of indecomposable modules (Tau Ceti exists_linearEquiv_directSum_isIndecomposableModule), and by the uniqueness part of the Krull–Schmidt theorem (Tau Ceti exists_equiv_linearEquiv_of_directSum), applied to the two resulting decompositions of A ⊕ C ≅ B ⊕ C, every isomorphism class of indecomposable modules occurs equally often in A and in B; hence A ⊕ C ≅ B ⊕ C implies A ≅ B; this leaves Sym^a ⊗ Sym^b ≅ ⊕_{i=0}^{b} det^i ⊗ Sym^{a+b−2i}.

End(Sym^{n−1}V) ≅ Sym^{n−1}V ⊗ (Sym^{n−1}V)^∨, (Sym^{n−1}V)^∨ ≅ Sym^{n−1}(V^∨) because the pairing between the symmetric powers of V and of V^∨ is perfect when (n − 1)! is invertible, and V^∨ ≅ V ⊗ det⁻¹ for V of rank two (R01.1/restriction-dual-tensor-twist); apply the first part with a = b = n − 1 and twist by det^{−(n−1)}.
acceptance: n = 2, p odd: End(V) ≅ k ⊕ Sym²V ⊗ det⁻¹.
n = 3, p ≥ 5: End(Sym²V) ≅ k ⊕ Sym²V ⊗ det⁻¹ ⊕ Sym⁴V ⊗ det⁻² (dimensions 9 = 1 + 3 + 5), for every Γ; this is the decomposition used for Sym²(SL₂(F_11)) in G7/enormous-symmetric-powers.
Outside the range nothing is claimed: for p = 2 and a = b = 1, V ⊗ V ≇ Sym²V ⊕ det for SL₂(F_2) acting on F̄_2² (G7/pieri-splitting-for-symmetric-powers, acceptance).

sources.locator: proof of Lemma 2.5.2, Publ. IHÉS 108, p. 56
sources.match: The decomposition of ad Sym^{n−1} for SL₂(F_l), which the source deduces from Serre's semisimplicity theorem; here it is proved for every Γ from the Pieri splitting.

nodes.title: Irreducibility of small symmetric powers of SL₂(F) and the one-dimensional constituents of their adjoints
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime and F a finite field of characteristic p, with SL₂(F) acting on F̄_p² by the standard representation. (a) For 0 ≤ a ≤ p − 1, Sym^a(F̄_p²) is an absolutely irreducible representation of SL₂(F); hence if r̄ : Γ → GL₂(F̄_p) has SL₂(F_p) ⊆ r̄(Γ) and 1 ≤ n ≤ p, every twist of Sym^{n−1} r̄ by a character is absolutely irreducible (Boxer–Calegari–Gee 2025, proof of Theorem 2.1). (b) (ibid., p. 514, where p > 5) Let p ≥ 5. For 0 ≤ i ≤ p − 1, the one-dimensional composition factors of Sym^{2i}(F̄_p²) as an SL₂(F)-module occur with multiplicity at most one, and only for i = 0, for 2i = p + 1 (only when F = F_p) and for 2i = 2p − 2. (c) (ibid., pp. 513–514) Let p > 3, 1 ≤ n ≤ p, r̄ : G_Q → GL₂(F̄_p) continuous with SL₂(F_p) ⊆ r̄(G_Q), and ρ̄ = Sym^{n−1} r̄ ⊗ ψ for a character ψ. Then every one-dimensional constituent χ of (ad ρ̄)^ss satisfies χ² = 1, and therefore H⁰(G_Q, M(1)) = 0 for every G_Q-subquotient M of ad ρ̄ or of its dual; in particular H⁰(Q, (𝔤⁰_n)^*(1)) = 0 for the Lie algebra 𝔤⁰_n = 𝔰𝔭_n or 𝔰𝔬_n of the similitude group preserved by ρ̄.
hypotheses: (a) fails for a = p: Sym^p contains the Frobenius twist of the standard representation as a proper submodule
(b) is about composition factors (semisimplification), not submodules
(c) needs p > 3 so that the mod p cyclotomic character satisfies ε̄^{−2} ≠ 1
(b) needs p ≥ 5: for p = 3 and F = F_3 the cases 2i = p + 1 and 2i = 2p − 2 coincide and Sym⁴ has the trivial character with multiplicity two
proofSteps: (a): Sym^a for a ≤ p − 1 is the restricted simple module L(a) of SL₂ over F̄_p and stays simple on SL₂(F) for every finite F ⊇ F_p (Steinberg restriction; Clozel–Harris–Taylor proof of Lemma 2.5.2 uses the same fact for F = F_l); twisting by a character preserves absolute irreducibility; the image r̄(Γ) contains SL₂(F_p).

(b): the only one-dimensional representation of SL₂(F) over F̄_p is the trivial one (SL₂(F) is perfect for #F ≥ 4, and SL₂(F_3)^{ab} has order 3). For 2i ≤ p − 1, Sym^{2i} is simple by (a) and trivial only for i = 0. For 2i = p + r − 1 with 2 ≤ r ≤ p − 1, G7/mod-p-clebsch-gordan-decompositions (b) gives the constituents of det^r ⊗ Sym^{p−r−1} (simple; trivial iff r = p − 1, i.e. 2i = 2p − 2) and of Frob V ⊗ Sym^{r−1}. If F = F_p then Frob V ≅ V and V ⊗ Sym^{r−1} ≅ Sym^r ⊕ Sym^{r−2} by part (a) of that node, which contains the trivial representation iff r = 2, i.e. 2i = p + 1. If F ≠ F_p, diag(z, z⁻¹) acts on Frob V ⊗ Sym^{r−1} through the characters z^{±p+s} with |s| ≤ r − 1 ≤ p − 2, and 0 < |±p + s| ≤ 2p − 2 < #F − 1, so no weight is trivial and there is no trivial constituent. For p ≥ 5 the values 2i = 0, p + 1, 2p − 2 are distinct, so each multiplicity is at most one.

(c): Boxer–Calegari–Gee: (𝔤⁰_n)^{*,ss} ⊆ (gl_n^*)^ss ≅ gl_n^ss ≅ ⊕_{i=0}^{n−1} (Sym^{2i} r̄)^ss ⊗ det(r̄)^{−i} (G7/mod-p-clebsch-gordan-decompositions (c)). A one-dimensional G_Q-constituent χ of this module factors through the projective image P of r̄, which contains PSL₂(F_p) and so is conjugate to PSL₂(k) or PGL₂(k) for a finite field k (R01.4/dickson-classification-and-the-dyadic-refinement); P^{ab} has order at most 2 (R01.4/normal-subgroups-and-automorphisms-of-psl2-pgl2 (a)), so χ² = 1; (b) says which summands contribute such a χ. As ε̄ has order p − 1 > 2 on G_Q for p > 3, χ ≠ ε̄^{−1}; and H⁰(G_Q, M(1)) ≠ 0 (a nonzero vector of Mathlib's Representation.invariants of M(1)) for a subquotient M would give the constituent ε̄^{−1} of M^ss.
acceptance: p = 7, F = F_7: Sym^0 = 1, Sym^8 (2i = p + 1) contains det-type constituent once, Sym^12 (2i = 2p − 2) contains one, and no other Sym^{2i} with i ≤ 6 has a one-dimensional constituent.
(c) fails for p = 3: ε̄^{−1} has order 2 and is self-dual, so the vanishing argument does not apply.
